articles.title: UK Inflation Reaches Nearly One-Year High as Rate Hike Bets Firm - TOKENPOST
articles.summary: UK Inflation Reaches Nearly One-Year High as Rate Hike Bets Firm  TOKENPOST
articles.full_text:
UK inflation accelerated to 3.5% in the year through September, reinforcing expectations that the Bank of England will raise rates at its Nov. 5 meeting.
Consumer prices rose from 3.1% in August, reaching their highest level since October 2025. The increase exceeded economists’ 3.4% expectation and left inflation above the Bank of England’s 2% target.
Transport prices were the biggest contributor to higher inflation in September, particularly motor fuel. Motor fuel prices were 30% higher than a year earlier, compared with a 23% annual increase in August. The Iran war and bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz have squeezed global oil and gas supplies.
The latest reading follows an earlier Bank of England policy outlook that focused on inflation control when UK inflation stood at 3.1%. The central bank held its main rate at 3.75% in September and signaled it was prepared to raise rates soon. Most economists expect the rate to reach 4% at the next meeting.
“With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise,” said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW.
UK Treasury chief John Healey said next week’s budget statement would aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from rising living costs. The Bank of England’s next meeting is scheduled for Nov. 5.

The gold rate in UAE today, October 22, 2026, remained unchanged during morning trading as investors balanced safe-haven demand arising from the Middle East conflict against the risk that higher oil prices could keep global interest rates elevated.
The Dubai price of 24-carat gold held at AED 497.25 per gram, while 22-carat gold remained at AED 460.50. Internationally, spot gold moved closer to the important $4,100 support level as higher energy costs, Treasury yields and uncertainty surrounding the Federal Reserve’s next decision limited buying interest.

At the published benchmark, 10 grams of 24K gold would cost approximately AED 4,972.50. A similar quantity of 22K gold would cost AED 4,605, while 10 grams of 18K gold would cost AED 3,785.
These calculations exclude jewellery-making charges, retailer margins and any applicable taxes. Final shop prices can therefore differ from the benchmark rate.
Spot gold declined approximately 0.4% to $4,123.25 per ounce during early Asian trading, bringing the metal closer to $4,100, an important short-term support level.
Higher Treasury yields and a firm US dollar continued to create resistance for bullion. Because gold does not provide interest income, its relative appeal can weaken when government bonds offer higher yields.
Nevertheless, geopolitical uncertainty is preventing a larger decline. Further escalation in the Middle East could increase demand for assets perceived as stores of value, particularly if attacks begin to materially affect energy production or regional trade.
The result is a conflicted market: interest-rate expectations are pressuring gold, while geopolitical risk is providing support.
Brent crude rose 1.1% to approximately $110.06 per barrel, while WTI gained 1% to $98.08 after fresh attacks raised concerns about Middle East supply disruptions. WSJ
Higher oil prices can affect gold in two opposing ways.
On the bullish side, expensive energy increases inflation risk and can encourage demand for gold as a hedge against the declining purchasing power of money. Conflict-driven oil rallies can also increase demand for safe-haven assets.
However, higher oil prices may also encourage central banks to keep interest rates elevated. If energy costs spread into transportation, manufacturing and consumer prices, policymakers may delay rate cuts or consider additional tightening.
That reaction can be bearish for gold because higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.
This second effect has recently dominated the market. Gold has struggled to benefit fully from Middle East tensions because investors are concerned that oil above $110 could prolong restrictive monetary policy in the United States and other major economies.
The Federal Reserve will hold its next policy meeting on October 27–28. It raised the federal funds target range to 3.75%–4.00% in September, marking its first increase in three years.
Futures markets currently assign only about a 14.9% probability to another increase in October. That probability has fallen sharply from 57.5% a month earlier following cautious comments from several Fed officials.
A pause is therefore the market’s base case, but the policy statement and Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference will remain important. Investors will look for signals about whether persistent inflation and high oil prices could produce another increase in December.

For jewellery buyers, the current price is below several recent October readings but is not the lowest level recorded this month. The October 14 rate of AED 492.75 for 24K gold was AED 4.50 cheaper per gram.
That difference would equal AED 45 on a 10-gram purchase before making charges. Buyers making large purchases may therefore benefit from comparing both benchmark rates and retailer fees instead of focusing exclusively on the daily gold price.
Short-term buyers should also consider the possibility of greater volatility around the Federal Reserve decision. A stronger dollar or hawkish policy message could produce a lower entry price, while a geopolitical escalation or dovish Fed signal could quickly push the 24K rate back above AED 500.

Inflation at 3.5% Puts These UK ETFs in Focus as BOE Hike Bets Mount
UK inflation has climbed to an 11-month high, reinforcing expectations that the Bank of England will deliver its first interest rate hike next month, in more than three years. Notably, consumer prices rose 3.5% in the 12 months through September 2026, up from 3.1% in August and above economists' forecasts of 3.4%, according to the Office for National Statistics.
The acceleration was driven largely by motor fuel costs, which surged 29.8% year over year — the fastest pace since August 2022 — as Britain's status as a net energy importer left it exposed to external shocks. To this end, markets are now pricing a 98% probability of a 25-basis-point hike to 4% next month, with traders also betting on a further increase at the central bank's final meeting of the year in December.
A rate hike reshapes the return calculus across UK equities, lifting bank margins, pressuring rate-sensitive sectors like real estate and consumer discretionary, and shifting gilt yields. The latest inflation hike puts UK stocks and by extension exchange-traded funds (ETFs) holding them squarely in the spotlight.
Before diving into those ETFs, it is worth understanding which industries stand to gain or lose from tighter policy (and why) so investors can make an informed decision.
Industries Stand to Gain or Lose
The UK's inflation rebound to 3.5%, combined with mounting expectations of a November rate hike, creates a sharply divergent picture across industries.
Direct beneficiaries of the rate hike will be banks and financial institutions. A hike widens net interest margins, which should act as a tailwind for major UK lenders such as HSBC, Lloyds, and NatWest. Near-term sentiment, however, may still be choppy, as expectations of higher interest rates have weighed on bank stocks amid concerns that tighter monetary policy could slow economic growth and increase credit losses. Investor anxiety over a potential increase in the bank tax surcharge in the upcoming Autumn Budget has added to the pressure.
Rate-sensitive industries like real estate and REITs are first in the firing line, as higher borrowing costs compress valuations. Retail and consumer discretionary face a tougher backdrop too; as unemployment at 4.7% and slowing real wage growth may push consumers to cut non-essential spending, leaving supermarkets and value retailers relatively more defensive.
As far as the Energy sector is concerned, the result is expected to be mixed. This is because while high oil prices lift energy earnings expectations, fuel inflation is itself the core driver of this hike, and eventual policy tightening could weigh on demand. As investors weigh both sides, BP and Shell’s share price movement will be in focus.
What Does This Mean for UK ETFs?
Against that industry backdrop, the ETF calculus is nuanced. A hike supports the pound and pressures long-duration bonds while widening net interest margins for lenders, making financials-heavy UK equity funds the clearer beneficiaries.
At the other end sit domestically focused consumer discretionary and real estate funds, which inherit the same headwinds as their underlying sectors as borrowing costs rise and household budgets tighten.
Currency-focused funds tracking sterling also come into play, gaining support from a hawkish BOE but exposed to volatility if the policy path shifts. Meanwhile, broad UK equity funds spanning the large-cap index offer the widest exposure to this rotation, though their sector mix determines whether they lean into the banking tailwind or the consumer and property headwind.

EWU has risen 8.6% year to date and charges 50 basis points (bps) in fees.

This fund, with a market value of $103 million, tracks the price of the British pound sterling.
FXB has slipped 0.8% year to date and charges 40 bps in fees.

This fund, with net assets worth $35.6 million, employs the AlphaDEX stock selection methodology to select 76 stocks from the NASDAQ United Kingdom Index. SHEL holds the first spot in this fund, carrying 2.82% weight, while Kingfisher holds the second position carrying a 2.60% weight.

TradingKey - During the Asian session on October 22, gold prices (XAUUSD) weakened further in intraday trade, with spot gold falling below the $4,100 mark to hit a low of $4,066.56, its lowest level since October 14. As oil prices have remained high recently, market concerns that energy prices will drive up inflation and extend the Federal Reserve's high-interest-rate cycle have intensified, leaving gold under continued pressure.
As of press time, intraday losses in spot gold briefly approached 2%, trading around $4,070. After consolidating around $4,100 for several consecutive trading days, gold prices officially broke below this key psychological level today, further expanding short-term downside pressure.
From a fundamental perspective, oil prices have been an important factor affecting gold price trends recently. Brent (UKOIL) crude oil recently reclaimed $110, with Middle East tensions keeping crude supply risks elevated. Higher energy costs could increase subsequent U.S. inflation pressure, prompting the market to continue assessing how long the Federal Reserve will maintain its restrictive monetary policy.
Regarding interest rate expectations, the Federal Reserve will hold its policy meeting on October 27–28. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, market expectations for another rate hike this month remain relatively limited, with traders pricing in an approximately 16% probability of an October rate hike; however, expectations for a December rate hike remain high, with a probability close to 90%. Higher real interest rate expectations increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold.

Currently, after gold fell below $4,100, it faces key support at $4,066 below. If this level is lost, gold will open up downside space toward $4,000; on the upside, it needs to reclaim $4,140 to relieve short-term downward pressure. Going forward, the market will focus on the Federal Reserve's rate decision and the latest U.S. PCE inflation data, both of which could further influence the U.S. dollar, interest rate expectations, and gold price movements.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average held its ground but the Nasdaq finished sharply lower Thursday as oil prices jumped on reports of planned U.S.-Israel strikes on Iran. Sellers hammered semiconductor firms of all stripes on the stock market today, while market leaders including Meta Platforms (META), FirstCash (FCFS) and biotech Moderna (MRNA) tanked.
The 30-stock Dow edged into positive territory before the close, ending 11 points higher at 52,867. But the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite skidded down 2.6% to 26,008. It fought to stay above the 26,000 level after reaching as low as 25,919 on Thursday. Alphabet (GOOGL) and Tesla (TSLA) losses were steep at 3% or more. Diversified chip designer Broadcom (AVGO) fell more than 4%. The Nasdaq-100 index was dragged down 2.8%.

The S&P 500 also lagged the Dow as it fell 1.2% to finish at 7,663. The large-cap benchmark notched a morning low of 7,637 and for most of the day it refused to stray far from that level. At that low, the S&P 500 remains up 11.5% year to date, excluding dividends. Some transport firms defied the selling, as railroad operator CSX (CSX) managed to steam toward a buy zone. CSX is up 6% so far this week.
West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures climbed more than 2% to around $99.20 a barrel on reports the U.S. and Israel have plans to strike Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
The 10-year Treasury yield plunged 19 basis points and undercut the 5% threshold to hit 4.95%. It was easily the largest single-session drop in the return for the long-dated debt security this year so far. Also, bitcoin sold off, sinking nearly 4% to trade around $81,300.
Volume shot higher vs. Wednesday on the New York Stock Exchange, early data showed. On a positive note, however, breadth was bullish as NYSE-based winners edged losers by a 4-3 margin.
Nasdaq turnover fell, but declining stocks outweighed advancing ones by almost a 4-3 ratio.
3:47 p.m. ET
Stock Market Today: A Broad Sell-Off
Within the MarketSurge Growth 250, Moderna (MRNA)collapsed on news that data regarding its melanoma cancer vaccine leaked ahead of a key business conference. Shares fell more than 23% in volume running double its average.
FirstCash (FCFS), a pawnshop operator and consumer loan chain, fell more than 13% and tripped below its rising 200-day moving average. Shares fell to 180, a six-month low. The Fort Worth, Texas-based company posted a 19% rise in third-quarter earnings, the smallest year-over-year increase in the bottom line in seven quarters. Sales growth also decelerated. The top line rose 18% to $1.1 billion.
Industry peer EZcorp (EZPW) fell in sympathy. The stock, down 10% in massive turnover, battled to hold around its own 200-day line.
Commodity stocks and companies tied to the buildout of AI data centers also fizzled.
GE Vernova (GEV) dived more than 11%, hitting a session low of 815.02. The supplier of natural gas and wind-based turbines and power generation equipment was making its first drop through the 200-day moving average since April 2025. The megacap industrial firm is also trading more than 12% below its sliding 10-week moving average, the red line plotted in the above chart. GEV has now extended its decline from a 1,195.94 all-time high to more than 31%.
Southern Copper (SCCO), whose products go into the wiring of a host of electric-powered devices, also undercut its 200-day moving average with a 7% pounding. The stock now lies 17% below a potential base's breakout point of 220.78.
On the upside, industrial chemicals giant Sasol (SSL) marked its third gain in four sessions, rising 7.4% and notching a three-year high of 17.45.
The South African member of Investor's Business Daily's oil and gas-refining and marketing industry group has now entered the 20%-25% profit zone from a 14.37 buy point. Its long base started in early May.
1:29 p.m. ET
These Stocks Buck The Drop
CSX (CSX), a major railroad operator, jumped 7% and approached a 52.15 early entry within a 12-week base. The base shows some elements of a double bottom.
CSX reported a 30% increase in profit for the third quarter vs. a year earlier to 57 cents a share. That marked the biggest year-over-year increase in more than four years. Strong demand for its shipment services in the light of rocketing diesel prices have helped CSX post three straight quarters of double-digit growth. Sales also accelerated vs. recent quarters, rising 12% to $4.02 billion.
The Dow Jones transportation average outperformed most indexes in the stock market today, rising 1.4%. Trading near 20,209, it is a small gain away from rebounding back above its 50-day and 200-day moving averages.
Meanwhile in the insurance industry, Dow stock Travelers (TRV) broke out.
Shares rose nearly 2% and moved past a 398.69 pivotal buy point in a 12-week flat base. The 5% buy zone goes up to 418.62. Thus, Travelers is in buy range.
The insurance and financial services titan recently reported a 13% gain in Q3 earnings to $9.18 a share amid flat sales of $11.5 billion. That stretched the New York City-based firm's double-digit bottom-line growth streak to six quarters in a row. Pretax margin rose 30 basis points to 19.1%, according to MarketSurge data.
Among biotechs, Amgen (AMGN) rallied nearly 2% in active trading and neared a 447.03 buy point in a cup-style base. Third-quarter results are expected on Nov. 3.
12:20 p.m. ET
Stock Market Today: This Sector Gets Thumped
Among exchange traded funds, the Invesco QQQ (QQQ) gave up 2.4%. Also, the State Street SPDR S&P 500 (SPY) fell 1.4%. Small caps outperformed, with the Russell 2000 down less than 0.1%.
Semiconductor and chip equipment companies were throttled by investors as the third-quarter earnings season heats up.
The VanEck Semiconductor (SMH) exchange traded fund nose-dived 5% and marked a 2-1/2-month low of 525.50. Six sessions earlier, SMH crashed through its 50-day moving average, hitting a defense-type sell rule.
The fund is now trading more than 21% below a 671.83 all-time high. Put another way, semiconductor companies have been digesting strong long-term gains since the early summer.
Within the chip equipment group, Lam Research (LRCX) notched its 13th decline in 14 sessions. Shares fell 10% to a six-month low of 232.20. Volume spurted more than quadruple its usual pace.
On average, the stock trades 8.7 million shares a day. Before noon, the volume already surpassed 9.4 million shares.
The wafer-fabrication equipment and services expert posted solid earnings of $2.20 per share in the September-ended fiscal first quarter, up 75% vs. a year earlier, as sales accelerated 54% to $8.22 billion. In the prior three quarters, the top line grew 22% to 30%.
However, the Fremont, Calif.-based company issued a fiscal second-quarter earnings forecast of $2.33 a share at the midpoint, with a revenue target of $8.6 billion. Wall Street predicts earnings of $2.35 a share and sales of $8.645 billion.
Lam is now trading nearly 47% off its high of 438.50. This means Lam must rally at least 87% just to match that peak. The stock is also spending its sixth-straight session hanging underneath its rising long-term 200-day moving average.
10:59 a.m. ET
Megacap Techs Drag Nasdaq Lower

US Treasury yields remained largely unchanged on Wednesday as investors waited for fresh economic data to understand the health of the US economy. The data could offer clues about the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision, which is scheduled for next week.
The 10-year US Treasury yield stayed at 5.1211%. This yield is closely watched because it influences borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards. The 2-year US Treasury yield held steady at 4.7889%. This yield is more closely linked to expectations about the Federal Reserve’s short-term interest rate decisions, according to CNBC.
30-year US Treasury yield holds steady

Key Moments
- EUR/USD trades with mild gains around 1.1235 in early Asian hours on Thursday, despite French political and fiscal headwinds.
- French 10-year OAT yields briefly touch 5% for the first time in 24 years before easing to 4.99%, underscoring mounting fiscal concerns.
- Fed sentiment remains firmly hawkish at 127.51 on the FXS Fed Sentiment Index, even as Chair Warsh strikes a slightly softer tone.
Euro Inches Higher Despite French Political and Fiscal Turbulence
EUR/USD is trading with a slight positive bias near 1.1235 in the early Asian session on Thursday. The pair is holding modest gains, though further upside appears constrained by intensifying political and fiscal tensions in France. Market participants are also awaiting remarks from European Central Bank (ECB) policymaker Fabio Panetta later in the day.
French sovereign borrowing costs have moved sharply higher, with the yield on the 10-year obligation assimilables du Trésor (OAT) rising more than 8 basis points to 5% on Wednesday, a level not seen in 24 years, before slipping back to 4.99%. The move reflects mounting unease over France’s fiscal trajectory and domestic unrest.
Financial markets have been rattled by the government’s inability to finalize a long-delayed budget, alongside widespread anti-government protests. These developments are clouding the near-term outlook for the common currency. French President Emmanuel Macron pledged to avert a repeat of last weekend’s riots and looting, as the Yellow Vest movement filed plans for a large march in Paris on Saturday that is expected to pose a major challenge for the administration.
“The French debt situation isn’t tractable. They do need to go in and make proper adjustments on the fiscal side to get this debt level down to at least show the seriousness around the trajectory,” said John Hardy, global head of macro strategy at Saxo in Copenhagen.
Rate Expectations: Limited Fed Hike Probability Near Term
In US markets, Fed funds futures indicate that traders are assigning only a small probability to a Federal Reserve rate increase at next week’s meeting. According to the CME FedWatch tool, the next potential move higher in policy rates is expected in December. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is also seen as unlikely to provide explicit guidance on future rate adjustments in the immediate term.
Euro’s Usual Links to Energy and Bonds Weaken
Analysts at Societe Generale observe that EUR/USD has displayed unexpected resilience. They note that “for EUR/USD, it’s curious that cycle highs in nat gas prices and bond jitters have not triggered another leg down in a way that would have occurred prior to October.”
The bank’s analysts point out that “the correlations have broken down over the past two weeks or so,” as the conventional relationships between EUR/USD, energy prices, and bond yields no longer match earlier patterns in the current cycle. They argue that this behavior “would suggest that most of the bad news is priced in or investors are not committed to putting on new directional trades, playing the ranges instead.”
Fed Communication: Warsh Balances Optimism With Crisis Scars
Fed Chair Warsh delivered a message that combined moderate optimism with caution. The FXS Speechtracker score for his latest appearance came in at 5.6/10, slightly below the usual baseline of 6.1/10, pointing to a somewhat less forceful tone.
Warsh acknowledged being “over-scarred from the Global Financial Crisis,” underlining an enduring bias toward risk aversion. At the same time, he highlighted structural growth dynamics and an investment upswing supported by “good policies,” while emphasizing that the upcoming October and December meetings will be the “crystalizing moment” for key decisions on output, employment, and inflation.
His comments also emphasized artificial intelligence as a near-term demand driver with uncertain implications for employment. Warsh’s remarks on plans for a field hearing and new Fed task forces indicate an effort to capture the benefits of technological progress while addressing potential downside risks and safeguarding financial stability.
Despite the slightly softer tone, the FXS Fed Sentiment Index was unchanged, moving 0.00 points to stay at a hawkish 127.51, comfortably above the neutral 100 mark. This combination suggests that markets are likely to interpret Warsh’s message as consistent with a framework that maintains a high threshold for easing, balancing optimism about investment and AI-related productivity against crisis-era caution and a firm focus on inflation and tail risks.
EUR/USD Technical Picture: Bearish Bias Under Key Moving Average
On the daily chart, EUR/USD continues to exhibit a bearish short-term bias. The pair remains below the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and under the middle line of the Bollinger Bands, with price action consolidating in the lower half of the recent volatility band. The 14-day Relative Strength Index (RSI) is hovering around 41, below the neutral 50 threshold, indicating that selling pressure still dominates over recovery attempts.

|---|---|---|
| 1.1455 | 100-day SMA | Key resistance |

On the upside, the first notable resistance level is the Bollinger middle band near 1.1245. A break above that zone would expose the upper Bollinger band around 1.1370, ahead of the more decisive barrier at the 100-day SMA at 1.1455. On the downside, the next important support area is located at the lower Bollinger band near 1.1120. A clear move below that level would signal scope for an extension of the broader downtrend.
Euro Basics: Key Drivers and Market Role
What is the Euro?
The Euro is the common currency used by 20 European Union member states that form the Eurozone. It is the second most actively traded currency globally after the US Dollar. In 2022, it accounted for 31% of all foreign exchange trades, with an average daily turnover exceeding $2.2 trillion.
The EUR/USD pair is the most traded currency cross worldwide, representing an estimated 30% of all FX transactions. Other heavily traded Euro pairs include EUR/JPY at 4%, EUR/GBP at 3%, and EUR/AUD at 2%.
Role of the ECB in Shaping the Euro
The European Central Bank (ECB), headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany, serves as the central bank for the Eurozone. It sets interest rates and conducts monetary policy with the primary objective of maintaining price stability, which can involve containing inflation or supporting growth.
The ECB’s main policy lever is interest rates. Higher rates – or expectations of higher rates – generally support the Euro, while lower rates tend to weigh on the currency. Monetary policy decisions are taken by the ECB Governing Council at eight scheduled meetings each year. The Council consists of the heads of the Eurozone national central banks and six permanent members, including ECB President Christine Lagarde.
Impact of Inflation Data on the Euro
Eurozone inflation is tracked using the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP). When inflation rises more than anticipated, particularly if it exceeds the ECB’s 2% target, the central bank is pushed toward raising interest rates to restore price stability.
Comparatively higher interest rates versus other economies typically bolster the Euro by making Eurozone assets more attractive to international investors.

The European Central Bank (ECB) and the People's Bank of China (PBOC) maintain regular multi-channel exchanges, and deeper mutual understanding yields shared benefits amid extensive trade, technology and financial ties linking China and the euro area, according to a member of the ECB's executive board.
China and Europe are advancing financial connectivity through institutionalized central bank dialogue. The first annual governors' meeting between the PBOC and the ECB, held in Beijing in June 2025, established a high-level communication channel.
"We interact with the People's Bank of China in different venues," Philip R. Lane, member of the ECB's Executive Board, told Xinhua in an interview in Shanghai. "The more we understand one another, the more it benefits everyone."
Together with renewed bilateral currency swap facilities and joint work on green finance standards, this institutional mechanism underpins deeper China-Europe financial ties, while both sides demonstrate leadership in developing sustainable finance frameworks for global markets.
On green finance, Lane said both the ECB and the PBOC recognize the importance of the green transition and have led the Network for Greening the Financial System. "The PBOC and the ECB are leaders in that global effort," he said, describing their joint role as critical in adapting the financial system to the green transition and the risks posed by extreme weather events.
For cross-border payments, Lane said the G20 roadmap is the best way to advance global coordination. As issuers of two of the world's major currencies, China and the euro area stand to gain greatly from steady exchanges under the G20. Regarding China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, he said it is natural for China to develop local-currency settlement facilities given its rising weight in global trade.
A drone photo shows a cargo ship docking at Yangzhou Port to unload containers in Yangzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Meng Delong/Xinhua)
Lane, who attended the 2026 Bund Summit in Shanghai, said there is substantial interest in Europe in using China's open-weight AI models. He also expressed appreciation for how China is exploring ways to leverage AI within a regulated framework to manage downside risks.
China's gross domestic product grew 4.5 percent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics. Lane said China's economy is an important driver of the world economy. Its strong export performance creates positive spillovers: European consumers enjoy greater product variety with lower prices, and European manufacturers gain access to more intermediate goods. "More domestic consumption would benefit China and the euro area," he added.
Through pragmatic and productive discussions, China and the European Union have shown a willingness to deepen cooperation and work toward a stable, more balanced economic and trade relationship. The two sides agreed to continue discussing the possibility of lowering tariffs on certain goods under WTO rules and reached an understanding on the trade of hybrid vehicles consistent with WTO rules.
Recent agreements aim to adjust the pace of trade flows, enabling the European automotive sector to adjust "in a more gradual manner," Lane remarked. He voiced optimism over the outlook for China-EU trade and investment ties. "China's growing wealth also allows its savings to finance European investment, representing a financial spillover," he said.
Underpinned by renewable energy expansion that lessens fossil fuel dependence, government fiscal backing, and AI-fuelled investment and manufacturing improvements, the euro area economy has proved more resilient than expected, prompting the ECB to raise its 2026 and 2027 growth forecasts in September.
With energy prices and inflation rising sharply due to the conflict in the Middle East, Lane said policymakers aim to guide inflation back toward the 2-percent target while avoiding derailing economic expansion. He added the ECB has implemented two rate hikes and will not lock in future moves in advance.

articles.title: French borrowing costs overtake US amid budget turmoil
articles.summary: France’s bond market hit by another bout of selling as country recovers from weekend protestsFrench borrowing costs continued to rise on Thursday, as investors fret that France’s government is struggling to pass a federal budget after public protests gripped the country.France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 y...
articles.full_text:
French borrowing costs continued to rise on Thursday, as investors fret that France’s government is struggling to pass a federal budget after public protests gripped the country.
France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 years.
The yield on the French 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat) – rose by nine basis points to 5.089% in early trading on Thursday, its highest level since July 2022. It broke across the 5% threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002.
The move lifted France’s 10-year borrowing costs over the equivalent for US Treasury bonds for the first time since 2013.
The volatility comes as the French government struggles to pass a budget for next year, while the country recovers from widespread protests that turned violent last weekend.
Tens of thousands of people had attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille in recent days.
Public buildings were attacked, and thousands of shops and businesses were looted. The interior ministry said there had been nearly 2,400 arrests.
Meanwhile, a parliamentary gridlock has blocked plans by the president, Emmanuel Macron, to increase the state pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to rein in state spending.
France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP.
It comes as the country also grapples with higher inflation triggered by the war in Iran, with many governments with big debt piles coming under acute pressure.
Jim Reid, a market strategist at Deutsche Bank, said the sell-off in French government bonds was starting to ripple out to other countries, too.
“Among others, the Italian 10-year spread over [German bonds] widened 3.8 basis points to 116 basis points, while Spain’s widened 3.1 basis points to 66 basis points, marking its widest level since June 2025,” he said.
Carsten Brzeski of the bank ING said rising yields had reinforced the European Central Bank’s “restrictive” monetary policy stance before its interest rate decision next week. The bank last raised its key interest rate to 2.5% in September.
“The ECB is very likely to stay on hold next week and will delay any next rate hike decision to December,” he said.
“Any solution to the current French fiscal woes could bring some relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to continue hiking rates. Without any solution, bond markets have taken over the ECB’s role, making rate hikes less likely.”

- Lower oil exposure: The euro zone economy is about half as reliant on oil as in the early 1990s, ECB economists estimate.
- Stronger fiscal support: Fiscal stimulus reached 0.5% of GDP, twice the level expected at the end of last year.
- Temporary growth drivers: ECB economists warn that AI investment, global demand and government spending may fade.
The euro zone economy has proved more resilient to this year’s energy shock than expected, according to European Central Bank (ECB) economists. Lower fossil fuel dependence, artificial intelligence investment and stronger government spending have helped sustain growth despite higher oil and gas prices.
Energy Dependence and Economic Resilience
ECB economists Oscar Arce, Gerrit Koester and Beatrice Pierluigi published the assessment in an ECB blog on Wednesday. They estimated that the euro area now relies on oil about half as much as in the early 1990s. This reduction has limited the economic impact of rising energy prices.
The Iran war disrupted energy markets, pushing oil and gas prices higher and renewing inflation concerns. However, the currency bloc has continued expanding, with business surveys showing that economic activity remains positive. Higher renewable and nuclear electricity generation has also weakened the connection between gas prices and electricity costs in several countries.
AI Investment and Fiscal Support
The ECB economists identified AI-related trade as an “important tailwind” for the euro area. Technology-related export orders and sectors linked to AI have outperformed, supporting economic activity during the energy shock.
Government spending has also exceeded earlier expectations. The fiscal impulse reached 0.5% of gross domestic product, twice the level projected at the end of last year. German government spending on defence and infrastructure accounted for much of the additional support.
However, the economists cautioned that several growth drivers could prove temporary. Global demand, fiscal stimulus and AI investment may weaken, particularly if geopolitical tensions intensify or energy markets face further disruption.
Monetary Policy Implications
The findings arrive as the ECB considers further interest rate increases to contain energy-driven inflation. A third rate increase this year is expected in December, following renewed inflation pressures and a global bond selloff.
The ECB assessment identifies reduced oil exposure as a structural source of resilience, alongside shorter-term support from investment and fiscal policy. However, its economists warn that fresh energy disruptions could leave the euro area vulnerable if those temporary sources of growth weaken.

articles.title: Asian shares wobble as tech rout boosts bonds, dents rate hike bets - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Asian shares wobble as tech rout boosts bonds, dents rate hike bets  The Edge Malaysia

SYDNEY (Oct 23): Asian shares fell on Friday as concerns over the enormous funding needs of artificial intelligence (AI) hammered tech and led to the biggest daily rally in Treasuries in more than three years, with investors fleeing to sovereign bonds and safe-haven currencies.
Markets also sharply pared back expectations of further policy tightening from the US Federal Reserve, stripping out almost a full quarter-point rate hike for next year amid concerns a bursting AI bubble could derail the data-centre investment boom and hobble the US economy. A December rate rise is no longer fully priced, with the implied probability falling to 85%.
That was despite elevated oil prices, with Brent hitting a five-month peak at US$114 a barrel on Friday. Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies as fears grow that the conflict in the Middle East could escalate sharply.
MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares excluding Japan fell 0.3% on Friday, bringing its weekly loss to 2.7% and marking a fourth straight week in the red. Japan's Nikkei dropped 1.3% and was down a whopping 5% for the week.
South Korea's Kospi skidded 1.7%, on course for a 4.3% weekly decline, with memory chipmaker SK Hynix down 2.5% on the day. Taiwan's stock market was closed due to a typhoon.
An index of mainland Chinese blue chips lost 1.1% on Friday to hit the lowest level since July 2025. The index was down about 20% from its peak in late June. Hong Kong's Hang Seng edged up 0.1% after dropping 3% on Thursday.
"AI is under the cosh," said Charlie McElligott, the managing director for cross-asset strategy at Nomura Securities International in New York, in a note.
"US Treasury bonds are — gasp — working as your hedge again, as the market seems to be real-time repricing the probabilities of a US growth scare off the back of the AI reset."
On Wall Street, the Nasdaq slumped more than 2% as Meta shares lost nearly 8% after the Facebook parent posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures, and announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the technology.
Tesla shares fell 3.1% as the electric car maker cut its 2026 capital spending plans.
"The question is whether selling accelerates or markets stage another familiar reversal," said Chris Weston, the head of Research at Pepperstone.
"There's nothing more emotive than a falling market where buyers refuse to engage. Sellers don't need a fresh catalyst when deteriorating price action itself encourages more selling."
As equities tumbled, money flowed into safe-haven US Treasuries, sending yields plunging across the curve overnight. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield slid more than 19 basis points, the biggest drop since March 2023, before steadying at 4.9591% on Friday, back below the closely watched 5% level.
That was also due in part to the ongoing sell-off in French bonds, whose benchmark yield climbed six basis points overnight to 5.0601%, the highest level since 2002.
"The US 10-year yield gapped back below 5% with some conviction. We are not convinced it keeps on going," said Padhraic Garvey, ING's regional head of research for the Americas.
"We're minded to expect it to snap back above [5%], as we still have inflation/fiscal deficit/AI boom underpinnings to navigate. And we have the US midterm elections approaching as an excuse for trouble. But it will need some degree of calm in the risk space first."
The two-year Treasury yield slumped nearly 19 bps overnight and were last flat at 4.6566%.
Government bonds in Asia also rallied. The yield on 10-year Japanese government bonds fell nine basis points to 2.790%, while Australia's 10-year yield dropped 10 bps to 5.164%.
In currency markets, safe havens such as the yen and Swiss franc gained. The dollar fell 0.2% to 156.44 against the yen on Friday, after slumping 0.9% overnight.
The dollar also slipped 0.1% to 0.8196 Swiss francs, the lowest in a month, after an overnight fall of 0.5%.
Gold failed to catch any safe-haven demand though, and was flat at US$4,021.99 an ounce on Friday after a nearly 3% drop overnight.

articles.title: Rising Bond Yields and Bank Stocks: Buying opportunity or risk? - www.sc.com

Table of Contents
“Net, net, it’s a positive for us” – that is how one global bank CFO described the impact of higher interest rates on the bank’s earnings. The same CFO, and many others, would also quantify how sensitive the bank’s income is to a shift in interest rates or the yield curve to estimate the potential uplift in earnings.
In September 2026, the US 10-year government bond yield rose to a 19-year high, posting its sharpest monthly increase since September 2022. Given that rising bond yields typically boost bank income, the recent moves should have ideally provided a strong tailwind. However, instead of rising with the yields, the global financial sector, including banking stocks, came under pressure and underperformed global equities.
This apparent contradiction highlights a more complex story at play. While higher bond yields can support bank revenues, several competing factors also create downside risks. Let us first consider where banks stand to benefit.
The upside from higher bond yields
Higher yields primarily lift bank earnings through wider net interest margins (NIMs). Banks can earn more on each dollar lent, and floating-rate loans can reprice upward quickly. At the same time, sticky deposit bases allow banks to pass on rate rises to savers more slowly, so margins widen.
In addition, a positively sloped yield curve – where longer-dated loans carry higher interest rates than shorter-dated loans – allows banks to fund themselves with short-term liabilities, such as customer deposits, and lend over longer periods through products such as mortgages. When the interest earned on these loans exceeds the cost of funding them, banks earn the margin. Importantly, any steepening of the yield curve can further widen this margin.
On the other hand, higher bond yields can pose risks as well.
The downside from higher bond yields
The most immediate hit is to the value of the bonds held by banks. Banks often invest their excess liquidity in bonds, whose prices fall as yields rise. The resulting mark-to-market losses could weigh on some banks’ capital ratios. These losses remain unrealised until banks sell the bonds – which they might be forced to do if deposit withdrawals surge. The realisation of such losses risk triggering a need for fresh capital – or if capital cannot be raised, it threatens a bank’s viability. Notably, these very dynamics were cited as one of the causes of several US regional bank failures in 2023 – a stark reminder that, for banks, customer confidence is critical.
Higher interest rates also increase borrowers’ debt-servicing burden, which can raise loan-loss provisions and reduce banks’ earnings. Higher rates can also lead to slower economic activity, dampening capital market activity and the demand for loans. Lower loan volumes, in turn, create a drag on banks’ interest income. Finally, if short-term yields rise faster than long-term yields, the yield curve ‘flattens’, narrowing the margin banks earn from borrowing short-term and lending long-term.
The current regional outlook and investment implications
With US bond yields having risen sharply over the past month to near two-decade highs, investors have become increasingly cautious about loan demand, capital buffers and funding costs. Yield curve dynamics have also shifted, with initial yield curve flattening (bad for banks) giving way to recent steepening (good for banks). Meanwhile, Euro area banks have faced additional headwinds from political and fiscal uncertainty in France.
The good news is that major banks remain well capitalised across the US, Europe and Asia. We believe sector fundamentals are largely intact and should continue to support strong earnings growth across the financial sector. We see particularly attractive opportunities in Euro area and Japan banks. For Euro area banks, a ‘higher-for-longer’ rate backdrop should extend the earnings upcycle. We also see earnings growth broadening to fee income. Combined with strong capital ratios and improving profitability, this backdrop supports higher dividends and share buybacks. Solid consensus earnings growth forecasts of 19% in 2026 and 12% in 2027, alongside reasonable valuations, strengthen the case for sustained sector performance.
In Japan, monetary policy normalisation by the Bank of Japan should drive NIM expansion, while a reflating economy boosts nominal loan demand. Corporate governance reforms – driving dividend growth and share buybacks – should enhance return on equity and support a continued valuation re-rating. Consensus earnings growth forecasts of 40% in 2026 and 16% in 2027 should provide further support.
As we embark on the Q3 2026 earnings season, we will continue to assess whether banks’ earnings and underlying fundamentals can sustain their growth momentum into 2027. Results from major US banks so far have been mixed relative to investor expectations but still point to a resilient US economy supported by strong business investments and consumer spending. Capital market activities are growing, although some lofty expectations have to be adjusted. Overall credit quality continues to be manageable.
Key risks to this constructive outlook include unexpected and significant loan losses, a broader slowdown in economic activity and heightened geopolitical tensions.

Canadian borrowing is losing steam just as interest rate hikes come back into focus. Bank of Canada (BoC) data shows mortgage credit posted its smallest August increase since 2013, pushing annual growth to a pace rarely seen outside housing corrections. With nearly a third of new mortgages carrying variable rates, renewed tightening could further throttle slow activity.
Canadian Mortgage Debt Growth Slows To Weakest August Since 2013
Canadian household debt: Residential mortgage credit, annual growth rate.
Source: Bank of Canada; Better Dwelling.
Residential mortgage debt advanced 0.3% (+$7.1 billion) to $2.45 trillion in August. That was unusually slow, marking the smallest August increase since 2013. Annual growth decelerated for a tenth straight month, leaving the balance only 3.8% (+$89.1 billion) higher than last year. It’s a slump that’s catching the attention of at least one Big Six economist.
“In August, household mortgage debt grew just 3.8% y/y, the slowest pace since the worst of the housing correction in 2023-24 (and before that, since the early 2000s),” explained Shelly Kaushik, senior economist at BMO Capital Markets.
Ontario & BC Slump, Weak New Condo Demand Slows Growth
The weak credit growth serves as a reminder that market stabilization isn’t the same as normalization. While the national market is stabilizing, it’s masking the prolonged slump in BC and Ontario. Weak demand in these regions, along with weak new condo demand in general, “has kept a lid on the recent recovery in borrowing,” according to Kaushik.
The data highlights another area the Bank of Canada (BoC) may be watching, explains Kaushik. “Canadian monthly credit aggregates, which typically fly under the radar, highlighted an ongoing slowdown in the economy’s most interest-rate-sensitive sector just as the Bank of Canada may be looking more closely at raising rates.”
Rate Hikes May Add To Mortgage Payment Stress
Bond yields are surging higher, but housing demand remains relatively weak. “Suffice it to say the housing market isn’t exactly in need of extinguishing,” says Kaushik. Variable-rate loans accounted for roughly 30% of new mortgages in Q2, according to BoC data cited by BMO, leaving those borrowers exposed to renewed rate hikes.
“Indeed, a new tightening cycle could add payment stress to variable rate mortgage holders,” she warns. Mortgage borrowing is already struggling to regain momentum. Renewed tightening could add further pressure to both the recovery and the households carrying that debt.

articles.title: Fed sneezes, but emerging markets aren’t catching a cold yet - BusinessWorld Online
articles.summary: Fed sneezes, but emerging markets aren’t catching a cold yet  BusinessWorld Online
articles.full_text:
By Jamie McGeever
ORLANDO, Florida — Emerging markets (EM) have developed stronger immune systems. US debt dynamics are deteriorating, and the Federal Reserve has started hiking interest rates, yet EM appears under no pressure to follow suit. The US has sneezed, but EM isn’t catching the proverbial cold.
Historically, when the Fed starts tightening policy, emerging economies are forced to hike as well, even if their domestic economies aren’t strong enough to warrant it, due to currency concerns and debt dynamics. This has given rise to another market cliché: the Fed is central banker to the world.
But surprisingly resilient economic growth across emerging economies this year, sturdier fiscal fundamentals, and relatively high interest rates and bond yields are offering EM central banks a degree of flexibility. That could allow them to start cutting rates in the next year, or, at the very least, enable them not to follow the Fed in lockstep as it tightens.
RATE BUFFER
Emerging markets — like their developed peers — are currently beset by a host of risks stemming from geopolitical strife, trade frictions, the energy price shock, and AI bubble fears. But even though some EM countries are particularly vulnerable, either to persistently high energy prices or a sudden, disorderly unwind of the AI trade, the threat of rapidly tightening monetary policy is mostly absent.
This is largely because policy rates are already elevated across much of the EM. The weighted average 10-year emerging bond yield at the end of September was around its highest point in five years at nearly 6.45%, according to State Street. Average inflation-adjusted EM yields, meanwhile, are also historically high, close to 3%.
Lofty policy rates have helped restore EM central bank credibility, support exchange rates, and create a real rate buffer. Bank of America strategists say EM rates at the front end of the curve have “materially” overshot to such an extent that implied policy rates next year will be in restrictive territory in all major emerging economies except China.
“Widespread tightening seems unlikely,” State Street strategists wrote earlier this month.
While EMs look surprisingly calm, robust, and attractive — with some notable exceptions like Indonesia — the same cannot be said of their developed-market peers.
While many emerging countries appear to be strengthening their economic fundamentals, investors’ concern over the fiscal trajectory in the US, Japan, much of the euro zone, and the UK has sent yields across the industrialized world to the highest in decades.
PIQUE INTEREST
Investors are positioning accordingly. A JPMorgan survey of investors at the International Monetary Fund/World Bank meetings in Bangkok last week showed that 33% favor EM stocks, compared with 26% who prefer developed market equities. Bank of America’s latest fund manager survey shows that a net 34% of those polled are overweight in EM stocks, down slightly from 38% in September, but hardly bearish.
Could investors be too optimistic about EM? Perhaps. The long EM equities position is one of the most crowded trades in BofA’s survey, suggesting there is still plenty of room for it to be trimmed further.
Of course, EM bond yields are higher because EM debt is still a riskier proposition than developed market offerings, especially traditionally “risk-free” US Treasuries. But it is notable that realized volatility in EM bonds has been lower than that of Treasuries for a few years, according to iShares benchmark EM bond and Treasuries ETFs.
To be sure, emerging economies’ debt burden is rising, narrowing the gap with highly indebted advanced economies. But the average EM debt-to-GDP ratio still appears manageable. The IMF projects an overall EM debt-to-GDP ratio this year of 77.2%, rising to 86.2% in five years, compared with forecasts for advanced economies of 108.2% this year, rising to 114.8%.
While the debt-to-GDP risk threshold in EM countries is lower because these economies are typically less resilient, few alarm bells are being rung. Indeed, the rise in EM debt has been quite gradual, suggesting policymakers are determined to keep it under control.
NOT A MONOLITH
Rising Fed rates and US market turbulence will always affect EM economies, especially those carrying more dollar-denominated debt. And there will always be idiosyncratic EM distress stories, like we’re currently seeing in Indonesia. But events like this typically bear little relation to the broader emerging market narrative. Removing Indonesia could actually make EM equity indices more attractive to investors.
It’s also important to remember that the EM universe is wide, and the differences between economies are vast. Policymakers in some EM countries where core inflation is relatively low and expectations are anchored, like Brazil and Mexico, are cutting rates, and some, like South Africa and South Korea, are raising them to offset currency weakness or inflation. Others may prefer to keep their options open.
But the Fed doesn’t appear to be calling the EM tune like it used to, and if the record attendance at Barclays’ EM Conference in Bangkok last week is any guide, that’s music to investors’ ears.

articles.title: IMF’s Krishna Srinivasan urges India to prioritise inflation as crude oil risks mount - Business Upturn
articles.summary: IMF’s Krishna Srinivasan urges India to prioritise inflation as crude oil risks mount  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
India should remain focused on controlling inflation as rising crude oil prices threaten to increase domestic costs and complicate economic management, according to the International Monetary Fund’s Asia and Pacific Department Director, Krishna Srinivasan. His remarks come amid continuing energy-market uncertainty and pressure on oil-importing economies, with higher international prices potentially affecting fuel costs, transportation, the rupee and household purchasing power. The policy challenge is to contain persistent price pressures without unnecessarily weakening economic activity.
Srinivasan’s recent comments on India’s response to the oil shock have also highlighted the importance of exchange-rate flexibility. Speaking at a media briefing in Mumbai on October 21, he said the IMF advised countries to use the exchange rate as the “first line of defence” against ongoing shocks and recommended allowing the rupee to move. He added that foreign-exchange intervention may provide only short-term relief when external pressures persist.
India’s exposure stems partly from its dependence on imported crude. According to a July 2025 analysis published in the Reserve Bank of India’s Bulletin, crude imports accounted for more than 85% of India’s oil requirements. The study estimated that a 10% increase in global crude prices could raise headline inflation by around 20 basis points, although government intervention has historically limited the pass-through to domestic prices.
Higher oil prices can affect the economy through several channels. More expensive fuel raises transportation and production costs, potentially feeding into prices of goods and services. It can also increase the import bill, put pressure on the current account and contribute to depreciation of the rupee. A weaker currency may make imported energy more expensive in rupee terms, adding to inflationary pressure.
The IMF has warned more broadly that a prolonged energy shock could weigh on Asian growth while increasing inflation and tightening financial conditions. In an April 2026 analysis, the Fund recommended anchoring inflation expectations, allowing prices to adjust where appropriate and providing temporary, targeted support to vulnerable households rather than relying on broad subsidies.
For India, the immediate challenge is balancing price stability with growth and protecting households from a renewed increase in essential costs. Any policy response will depend on the duration of the oil shock, domestic inflation data, currency movements and the government’s approach to fuel prices.
Markets and policymakers will watch global crude trends, the rupee’s movement and upcoming inflation readings for signs of whether energy costs are spreading into broader prices. The IMF’s position points to continued vigilance on inflation, alongside policies that strengthen energy security and reduce vulnerability to external shocks.

articles.title: Single-stock leveraged ETFs reignite turf war between financial regulators - The Korea Times
articles.summary: Single-stock leveraged ETFs reignite turf war between financial regulators  The Korea Times
articles.full_text:
A long-running turf war between Korea’s top financial regulator and financial watchdog is flaring up again over responsibility for the introduction of single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs), amid steep retail investor losses and heightened market volatility, according to market watchers Thursday.
The Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) labor union attributed the controversy to the agency’s lack of independence from the Financial Services Commission (FSC), bringing their recurring struggle over policymaking authority and supervisory autonomy back into focus.
Leveraged and inverse ETFs tied to Samsung Electronics and SK hynix began trading on the Korean stock market on May 27. The products have since come under fire over heavy investor losses and concerns about their impact on market volatility.
Figures submitted by the FSS to the National Assembly showed that retail investors at 10 major domestic brokerages incurred combined losses of 6.31 trillion won ($4.8 billion) between the launch and Aug. 14. Of that amount, 2.32 trillion won represented realized losses, while the remaining 3.99 trillion won, or 63.2 percent, consisted of unrealized losses.
At Monday’s parliamentary audit, FSS Gov. Lee Chan-jin acknowledged that the review process had been unusually rushed to accommodate the launch timetable set by the FSC.
The FSS union said Wednesday that the underlying problem lies in a system that subordinates supervision to government policy. With the FSC exercising oversight of the FSS and approving its staffing levels and budget, the agency faces institutional constraints on challenging policy decisions, the union argued.
“Even when government financial policies carry risks or reveal shortcomings, concerns about repercussions for the agency, including its budget, make it difficult to speak out,” the union said.
The union added that the FSS cannot enact or revise supervisory regulations or independently submit matters for the FSC’s consideration. Those restrictions hamper timely intervention when risks surface during policy implementation, it said.
“When those risks materialize and consumers suffer losses, responsibility ultimately falls on the FSS,” the union said. “The resulting scrutiny then leads to tighter government control, perpetuating a vicious cycle.”
Although both bodies are charged with maintaining financial market stability, they serve different functions. The FSC, the country’s top financial regulator, sets financial policy, promotes industry development and oversees regulatory reform. The FSS, a special statutory body, conducts examinations of financial companies, supervises their operations and protects consumers.
The FSC’s authority over the FSS’ organization and finances has made the relationship a persistent source of friction, particularly when policy objectives clash with supervisory concerns.
A notable confrontation arose during the 2018 accounting review of Samsung Biologics. The FSS determined that the company’s 2015 change in accounting treatment constituted deliberate accounting fraud. The FSC sought another review, saying further examination was necessary before a clear conclusion could be reached.
Tensions resurfaced earlier this year over a proposal to broaden the powers of the FSS’ special judicial police. The agency sought a wider investigative remit and the ability to open investigations into suspected unfair trading on its own initiative.
The FSC questioned whether a nongovernmental supervisory body should wield such extensive law enforcement powers, citing the potential for abuse and difficulties in ensuring adequate oversight.
The FSS union called for the FSC’s supervisory and budget approval powers over the FSS to be transferred to the National Assembly to strengthen the agency’s operational independence.
At Thursday’s parliamentary audit, meanwhile, both FSC Chairman Lee Eog-weon and FSS Gov. Lee apologized to the public over losses linked to single-stock leveraged ETFs.
“Despite the policy considerations and objectives behind their introduction, I feel a heavy sense of responsibility for the consequences,” the FSC chairman said. “We will take greater care and adopt more precise measures to protect investors and maintain market stability.”

PBOC: Role and Policy Mandate
The People’s Bank of China is tasked with maintaining price stability, which includes stability in the exchange rate, while fostering economic growth. In addition, the central bank is responsible for advancing financial reforms, such as the opening and development of China’s financial markets.
Ownership and Governance Structure
The PBOC is owned by the state of the People’s Republic of China and is therefore not regarded as an independent institution. Strategic direction and management are heavily influenced by the Chinese Communist Party Committee Secretary, who is nominated by the Chairman of the State Council rather than by the central bank governor. Mr. Pan Gongsheng currently holds both the role of CCP Committee Secretary and governor.
Key Monetary Policy Instruments
The PBOC employs a wide range of tools to pursue its policy goals, which differs from the approach typically seen in Western economies. Its primary instruments include the seven-day Reverse Repo Rate, the Medium-term Lending Facility, foreign exchange interventions, and the Reserve Requirement Ratio.
China’s benchmark interest rate is the Loan Prime Rate. Adjustments to the LPR directly affect borrowing costs for loans and mortgages, as well as returns on savings. Through changes in the LPR, the central bank can also exert influence on the value of the Chinese Renminbi in foreign exchange markets.
Presence of Private Banks in China
Private banks operate alongside state-controlled financial institutions within China’s banking sector. There are 19 private banks, representing a relatively small slice of the overall system. The largest among them are digital lenders WeBank and MYbank, backed by Tencent and Ant Group respectively, according to The Straits Times.
China opened the door in 2014 for domestically funded lenders fully capitalized by private capital to participate in the country’s state-dominated financial industry.

articles.title: Two Cheers For Kevin Warsh's "Quiet" Fed - RealClearMarkets
articles.summary: Two Cheers For Kevin Warsh's "Quiet" Fed  RealClearMarkets
articles.full_text:
Markets can't tell whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week. After September's inflation reportcame in hot at 3.7%, markets moved the probability of a hike from 20% to 50%. Within days, fed funds futures put itback near 20%. Commentators are irritated. Chairman Kevin Warsh has gone quiet, no longer telling them what comes next. The Fed's statements don't contain forward guidance anymore, and Warsh declines to submit his own interest rate forecast, calling it "not helpful in the conduct of policy."
The complaint is that nobody knows what the Fed will do. The complainers have missed the point of central banking. Predictability is good, but the Fed can't commit with any credibility to a specific interest rate quarters in advance. More importantly, only central banks without rules-based policy need to preannounce their decisions. It's the lack of rules that needs fixing.
Forward guidance was the Fed's ongoing preview about where rates were headed. It was sold as a transparency mechanism. But it was really a stand-in for something the Fed didn't want: a binding commitment. In the 1970s, economists Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott showed why benevolence and competence couldn't substitute for genuine rules. Credible monetary policy must constrain monetary policymakers. Low, stable inflation, with no sacrifice of employment, results when central banks tie their own hands in predictable ways.
By the 1980s that argument had won over most macroeconomists. But central bankers, living in the world of practical politics, found a way to avoid meaningful rules. What they adopted was what Ben Bernanke called "constrained discretion": rule-like behavior sometimes, with the central bank retaining the right to deviate according to its judgment about what the economy needed. The problem should be obvious: if policymakers get to decide when to follow a rule, the rule doesn't really constrain them.
As a result, the Fed regularly gets away with moving the goalposts. In December 2012 the Fed promised to hold rates near zero at least until unemployment fell to 6.5%. When unemployment got close, it dropped the threshold. In 2020 it promised to let inflation run above 2% to make up for past shortfalls. When inflation greatly exceeded 2%, it hand-waved away the surge as "transitory," and then scrapped the make-up strategy altogether. Each time the Fed said one thing and did another; each time its promises meant less. Inflation has now run above target for more than five years. American businesses and families, rather than monetary technocrats, ultimately pay the price of the Fed's cheap talk.
There's a deeper error here. The insight that reshaped economics half a century ago was not that the Fed should manage expectations by talking. Rather, it was that market actors form expectations from what the Fed actually does. Press conferences don't create credibility. Regime changes do. The Fed tried to get the benefits of fundamental institutional change from mere speech acts. But the public wasn't fooled.
Forward guidance rested on a false premise: that households and businesses need to know the Fed's policy rate quarters or years in advance. They don't. The interest rate is a price—the price of capital—and the whole point of a price is to move in conjunction with supply and demand. There's no way the Fed can make predictions that accurate. Pre-committing to a rate path means pre-committing to error, sooner or later.
What the public needs to know ahead of time is not the price of credit but the fundamental monetary yardstick: what a dollar will buy next year and the years after. Central banks are bad at controlling interest rates. In contrast, they are capable of controlling inflation when they're made to. Center the promise on the price level, which gives the economy what economists call a "nominal anchor," and interest rates will find their correct levels on their own.
Importantly, Warsh's silence is good only if it's a first step towards a stricter, rules-bound monetary regime. While not talking about the Fed's policy instrument is fine, not talking about the final goal of policy could be disastrous. Because households and businesses necessarily incorporate expectations about the dollar's purchasing power into their plans, the Fed can't afford not to have a rule. The only choice is between a vague, informal directive—like we have now with the dual mandate and data-dependent guesswork—and a dollar-stability rule with teeth.
Warsh has long argued the Fed talks too much. So far, Warsh’s Fed seems like it will focus much less on talking and much more on doing. His task forces on the Fed's framework and communications report by year's end. Let's hope they recommend the right way forward: a single price-stability goal, preferably with consequences for officials who miss it. Then the Fed can stop talking about rates for good, for the simple reason that nobody will need it to.

Oct 21 (Reuters) - Gold prices edged higher on Wednesday, rebounding from a near one-week low hit earlier in the session as weaker US Treasury yields lent support, while investors awaited next week's Federal Reserve meeting.
Spot gold was up 0.3% at $4,137.94 per ounce by 2:12 p.m. EDT (1812 GMT) after hitting its lowest since October 15 in earlier trade. US gold futures for December delivery settled 0.2% higher at $4,150 per ounce.
The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield fell for a second consecutive session, reducing the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold.
Investors are now focused on the Fed’s October 27-28 policy meeting and next week’s US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) report for clues on future rate moves.
"I think the market is currently expecting one 25-basis-point rate hike this year, but probably not until December. The likelihood of an October rate hike has dropped pretty significantly," said Peter Grant, vice president and senior metals strategist at Zaner Metals.
"I think gold prices will be range-bound for the time being. But I think the bias remains to the downside."
Markets are pricing in an 88% chance that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December, according to CME's FedWatch Tool.
Nearly all economists surveyed by Reuters expect the Federal Reserve to hold rates steady this month and raise them in December, as policymakers choose patience despite persistent inflation that would ordinarily warrant tougher action.
Although gold is traditionally considered an inflation hedge, higher rates dent its appeal as investors prefer yield-bearing assets.
"I would still believe in the short term, gold is in consolidation mode. So whenever we go below 4,100, it's bottoming out because there is buying interest, but the upside remains limited as long as the conflict in the Middle East is somehow still a topic," said Giovanni Staunovo, an analyst at UBS.
Meanwhile, oil prices were little changed as investors weighed possible progress toward Russia-Ukraine talks against declining US oil stocks and a lack of US-Iran dialogue.
Among other metals, spot silver slid 0.4% to $57.73 per ounce, platinum fell 0.9% to $1,633.65 and palladium dropped 0.9% to $1,092.75.
