articles.title: Is the bond market pricing in a policy error by the Federal Reserve? - Moomoo
articles.summary: Is the bond market pricing in a policy error by the Federal Reserve?  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
Imagine this: In early October, someone looks into a crystal ball and tells you that the upcoming September CPI data will exceed market expectations, with the Producer Price Index (PPI) rising by 1.3% for the month, far above the forecast of 0.5%. Beyond this bearish inflation news, they also mention that inflationary pressures are still building, and crude oil prices will rise by $10 in the first two weeks of the month. Based on this prediction, what level do you think the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note would reach? For reference, on October 1, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury was approaching 5.25%. We would bet that the vast majority of professional bond traders would wager on yields reaching 5.50% or even higher.
After the CPI data was released on October 14, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury surged rapidly, touching 5.33% within minutes of the announcement. However, just a few days later, the yield fell significantly to 5.03%. The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury also experienced a similar decline. Faced with inflation data that exceeded expectations—a bearish signal—the bond market instead saw a rally.
Mohamed El-Erian, former CEO of PIMCO and a renowned bond expert, raised this obvious question on the social media platform X:
Despite both CPI and PPI inflation data exceeding expectations, why are U.S. Treasury yields declining?
He offered two logical explanations. This article interprets his two AI-related analyses and adds two of our own perspectives. The most critical point is that the bond market may have already begun pricing in a risk: that the Federal Reserve might be forced into a policy error.
Explanation 1: Capital flows out of tech stocks and into safe-haven assets
The first driver identified by El-Erian is capital withdrawing from technology stocks, which had been on a sustained upward trajectory but are now under pressure, triggering safe-haven buying.
Many semiconductor stocks continued to weaken. Between October 1 and the release of the PPI data on October 15, the SOX Semiconductor Index fell by nearly 20%.
The Nasdaq Composite, which has a high weighting in semiconductors, declined in tandem. Overseas markets also suffered significant losses, including the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) and Japan's Nikkei Index, both of which have concentrated exposure to technology stocks.
As shown in the chart below, since October 1, the healthcare sector (XLV), consumer staples sector (XLP), and other value sectors that had previously been sold off have risen, while the technology sector (XLK) has moved in the opposite direction. This rotation is essentially a shift toward safe-haven assets within the equity market, but El-Erian argues that it has also generated some demand for Treasury bonds.
In addition, El-Erian noted that credit stress is emerging in the most vulnerable market segments. For instance, the debt yield of CoreWeave, a major data center service provider, surged from 9% to 15%. As investors demand such high yields for bonds issued by CoreWeave and its peers, there are growing concerns that CoreWeave could become the "canary in the coal mine" (an early warning signal) for the AI boom.
Such credit risk events often trigger a flight to safety, with capital shifting from corporate bonds to U.S. Treasury securities.
Interpretation 2: Is technology still the engine of economic growth?
El-Erian’s second point carries broader macroeconomic implications: AI-related capital expenditure has been a core driver of economic growth. If investors are no longer willing to fund AI expansion projects and companies themselves lack the capacity to bear these costs, will the outlook for economic growth consequently weaken?
Charu Chanana of Saxo Bank stated:
Investors are no longer willing to finance the expansion of AI infrastructure regardless of cost.
Against the backdrop of the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield breaking above 5% and credit spreads for some AI-related loans reaching junk-bond levels, financing costs for data centers have risen sharply. A contraction in AI capital expenditure implies slower GDP growth; downward revisions to growth expectations would then dampen inflation expectations, ultimately driving long-term yields lower.
Interpretation 3: Short covering and strong demand signals
The first point we add to El-Erian’s analysis is short covering. Entering October, the bond market was broadly betting on rising yields.
Citing data from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Bloomberg reported that in the week ended September 22, asset managers added more than 100,000 net short positions in 10-year U.S. Treasury futures, marking one of the largest weekly increases in short positioning since 2023. Furthermore, during the 14 trading days in late September, open interest in 10-year Treasury futures rose on 13 days, while open interest in 5-year Treasury futures increased on 11 out of 12 days. This indicates that as yields climbed, the market continued to build new short positions.
The auctions of 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury securities held on October 7 and 8 appeared to foreshadow the reversal in market trends. While many investors had anticipated weak demand for newly issued Treasuries, the outcome proved quite the opposite. As noted in our commentary:
Wednesday’s auction of $39 billion in 10-year notes concluded with a high yield of 5.300%, which was 1.7 basis points lower than pre-auction market expectations, indicating results that far exceeded market forecasts. The auction of $22.5 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday saw similar outcomes. As shown in the chart below (box plots provided by ExanteData), bidding data for both auctions deviated significantly from historical norms. The bid-to-cover ratio, representing the amount of bid capital received per $1 of new issuance, reached 2.77 for the 10-year notes, surpassing the 12-month average of 2.51 and marking a new high in nearly 50 auctions. The 30-year bonds recorded a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.54, above the historical median of 2.40, placing it in the upper range of the last 50 auctions.
Participation by primary dealers is perhaps the most critical indicator of these auctions. U.S. Treasury primary dealers are obligated to absorb any unsold bonds. A high proportion of dealer take-downs typically signals tepid auction demand, forcing Wall Street firms to hold inventory. In this instance, primary dealers took down only 2.5% of the 10-year notes, setting a historical low for this maturity; the dealer take-down rate for the 30-year bonds was 6.8%. Indirect bidders (mostly foreign central banks and domestic institutions) secured 80.3% and 72.3% of the respective allocations, figures well above historical averages.
The minimal need for primary dealer support in these auctions suggests that genuine long-term capital is absorbing Treasury supply at current yield levels. Although bond prices did not immediately rally following the strong auction results, the outcome serves as a warning to short sellers: market demand remains robust at yields above 5%. Strong buying pressure has prompted short sellers to buy back Treasuries to close their positions. Given the crowded nature of short positions in the market, this covering activity creates a feedback loop, forcing further short squeezes.
Explanation 4: The bond market senses the risk of policy errors
The bond market may be starting to believe that higher-than-expected inflation data this month will compel the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates further rather than cut them, ultimately leading to a policy error.
Changes in the shape of the yield curve over the past two weeks corroborate our assessment. On October 7, the spread between the 2-year and 10-year U.S. Treasury yields was 57 basis points. Following the release of CPI and PPI data, the spread narrowed to 32 basis points. This 25-basis-point compression over two weeks occurred largely on the day the inflation data were released.
When yields decline synchronously, with long-term yields falling more than short-term yields, this pattern is known as bull flattening. If the market expects the Federal Reserve to continue tightening policy amidst weakening economic conditions, capital flows into long-term bonds, driving the curve to flatten. Conversely, if the market fears runaway inflation, the trend will manifest as bear steepening.
The short end of the yield curve prices in the probability of Federal Reserve rate hikes, while the long end prices in the economic consequences of such hikes.
Reasons for concern over policy errors
Several factors are causing concern in the bond market regarding potential deviations in Federal Reserve policy:
First, the current rise in inflation is largely driven by supply shocks. The increase in gasoline and diesel prices stems from geopolitical tensions involving Iran, rather than overheating domestic consumption. While the Federal Reserve cannot increase oil production, it can suppress demand for all other goods.
Second, the labor market has weakened. Nonfarm payrolls increased by only 29,000 in September, with prior months’ data revised down by a cumulative 60,000. Furthermore, the unemployment rate has risen to 4.2%, while real incomes have remained flat or even declined slightly, providing little evidence of a wage-price spiral.

RBI rejects all bids at govt's T-bill auction as short-term yields surge
The yield on the benchmark 10-year government bond settled at 7.44 per cent, its highest level since November 4, 2022, against the previous close of 7.39 per cent
Listen to This Article
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Wednesday rejected all bids at the government’s treasury-bill (T-bill) auction, signalling discomfort with the sharp rise in short-term borrowing costs, dealers said. 
The yield on the benchmark 10-year government bond settled at 7.44 per cent, its highest level since November 4, 2022, against the previous close of 7.39 per cent. 
The central bank last rejected bids in June, when it cancelled auctions of 182-day and 364-day T-bills. At the end of March, it had rejected bids across all three maturities. 
The government had planned to raise ₹23,000 crore through the sale of 91-day, 182-day and 364-day T-bills. Traders said the yields sought by investors may have been higher than the RBI’s expectations. Government bonds, already under selling pressure due to rising crude oil prices and US treasury yields, were impacted further after the auction result. 
“The yield (on the benchmark 10-year government bond) will now inch up to 7.50 per cent from here. Crude remains the main overhang, with Brent trading around $112 per barrel, and US yields have also inched up. That is a worry for the market. Sentiment turned negative again after the auction result was announced,” said a dealer at a primary dealership. 
Also Read
Cutoff yields on T-bills have risen sharply over the past five weeks. Between September 9 and October 14, yields on 91-day, 182-day and 364-day bills rose by 64 basis points (bps), 83 bps and 69 bps, respectively. 
At last week’s auction, the government raised funds at yields of 5.73 per cent for 91-day bills, 6.29 per cent for 182-day bills and 6.49 per cent for 364-day bills. 
The spread between the yield on 364-day T-bills and the RBI’s policy repo rate widened to 99 bps last week, its highest level in four years, reflecting rising short-term borrowing costs.  
The central bank has turned decisively hawkish. It raised the repo rate to 5.50 per cent this month and shifted its stance to calibrated tightening, signalling the possibility of further increases. 
Bets on a 50 bps hike in December are growing, while the benchmark 10-year bond yield has risen around 20 bps since the policy announcement. 
Liquidity, which had cushioned the market for much of the year, has dried up. The RBI’s latest data showed that net liquidity in the banking system stood at a surplus of around ₹48,303 crore on Tuesday. 
Consequently, the RBI’s overnight variable rate repo (VRR) auction witnessed strong demand, with bids amounting to ₹93,241 crore against the notified amount of ₹50,000 crore. 
The weighted average call rate (WACR), the operating target of monetary policy, settled at 5.64 per cent on Wednesday, close to the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate, against 5.66 per cent in the previous session. On Monday, the RBI had conducted a ₹1 trillion VRR auction, the first in three months. 
“Liquidity has almost dried up, keeping overnight rates elevated. We also have tax outflows coming. The RBI would like to keep overnight rates aligned with the repo rate. That is why it is conducting these temporary liquidity infusions,” said a dealer at a state-owned bank. 
The turnaround in liquidity has been sharp. The RBI had been in absorption mode since August 6, following its last VRR auction on July 29, as liquidity had swelled due to Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank, or FCNR(B), deposit swaps with the central bank. 
Since then, the daily cash reserve requirement has been tightened from October 16. Average daily net absorption under the liquidity adjustment facility rose from ₹1.2 trillion in July to ₹5.8 trillion in August. As recently as October 12, the RBI absorbed a net ₹3.36 trillion, while the call rate stood at 5.41 per cent. 
The central bank plans to conduct another overnight VRR auction worth ₹50,000 crore on Thursday.

articles.full_text:
European wholesale natural gas prices advanced more than 3% on Wednesday as disruptions to energy shipments through the Persian Gulf and lower regional storage levels continued to affect supply conditions ahead of the winter heating season.
The benchmark Dutch TTF front-month contract rose 3.1% to €87.95 per megawatt-hour (MWh), while UK National Balancing Point (NBP) natural gas futures increased 3.2% to 216.57 pence per therm. Both contracts were trading near their highest levels since late 2022.
The price increases coincided with the publication of UK inflation figures showing that annual consumer price inflation reached 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August and above market expectations.
Higher energy import costs remain a consideration for the British economy, which relies on pipeline gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments to meet domestic heating and electricity generation requirements.
The UK's relatively limited long-term gas storage capacity also leaves the country dependent on continuing imports during periods of increased demand.
European gas benchmarks have recorded substantial gains since the beginning of 2026. Dutch TTF prices were approximately 210% higher year to date, while the UK NBP benchmark had risen around 196%.
Supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf have contributed to the increase in prices. Maritime strikes and restrictions affecting transit through the Strait of Hormuz have reduced the availability of LNG shipments from the Middle East.
According to the reported figures, Middle Eastern LNG deliveries to Europe were nearly 80% below their level a year earlier.
The reduction in available supplies has increased competition between European and Asian importers for LNG cargoes from the Atlantic basin, particularly those not already committed under long-term contracts.

articles.title: ETF inflows of $526.7 million meet a Bitcoin price of $82,708: the levels that decide before the Fed meeting - CryptoTicker
articles.summary: ETF inflows of $526.7 million meet a Bitcoin price of $82,708: the levels that decide before the Fed meeting  CryptoTicker
articles.full_text:

Select what genuinely interests you. Your picks feed directly into our editorial planning.
A Bitcoin costs $82,708 on Wednesday morning, or 73,652 euros. On Monday, $526.7 million flowed into the US spot ETFs, the strongest day since September, and yet October is still negative for those funds. Two lines frame the market until the Federal Reserve decides on rates on October 28: the 50-day moving average at $81,679 below, and the 20-day average at $83,117 above.
Overnight trading: the $81,273 low sat below the 50-day average
Between Tuesday morning and Wednesday morning the price moved between $81,273 and $83,249. That is a range of $1,976, or 2.39 percent measured against the current level. The night was therefore far livelier than the three days before it, which we covered on Tuesday.
Where the low sat matters more than the range itself. In our Tuesday morning piece, the 50-day average at $81,481 was the next level on the downside. That line has since risen to $81,679, an increase of $198. The overnight low of $81,273 sat $406 below it. The price broke the line and had worked its way back $1,029 above it by the morning.
In practice, that means a single breach has triggered no follow-on selling in this phase. Only a daily close below the line would be a signal that trading systems built on moving averages react to, and that did not happen overnight.
We calculated the moving averages in this piece ourselves, from CoinGecko daily closes over the past 200 days, as of Wednesday morning. Such lines differ by a few dollars between providers and data sources, because exchanges use different closing times.
$526.7 million into the US Bitcoin ETFs, the strongest day since September
According to Farside Investors data, the US spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $526.7 million net on Monday. That is the largest inflow on a single trading day since September. A spot ETF holds the coins itself rather than tracking the price through a futures position. Every dollar of inflow therefore leads to an actual purchase in the market.
The Ethereum ETFs ran the other way the same day and gave up $103.3 million, $95.4 million of it at BlackRock’s ETHA alone. So the money did not move broadly into crypto; it went into Bitcoin specifically.
BlackRock’s IBIT brought in $665.2 million, Fidelity’s FBTC lost $83.6 million
The net figure hides how uneven the day was. BlackRock’s IBIT alone took in $665.2 million, more than the entire net inflow for the day. Fidelity’s FBTC gave up $83.6 million over the same period.
A single provider carried the day, then, while at least one other lost money. Read the net figure as a broad return of institutional buyers and you are reading in more than the breakdown supports. For the price effect that is secondary: the coins have to be bought in the market, whichever provider receives the money.
October stays around $88 million in the red despite Monday
One strong day does not turn the monthly balance. On the daily Farside Investors figures, which the financial service FXStreet reviewed on Tuesday, the US spot Bitcoin ETFs remain around $88 million in the red for October. Monday almost evened out the month, no more than that.
That fits the price picture. Bitcoin is down 1.16 percent over seven days and up 1.56 percent over 30 days. It sits 34.4 percent below the all-time high of $126,080 from October 6, 2025. The market has been moving sideways for weeks, and the fund flows are doing the same.
The 200-day average at $72,723 and a gap of 13.73 percent
The short averages sit close to the price, but the distance to the downside is wide. On our calculation the 200-day average stands at $72,723, with the price 13.73 percent above it. The 100-day average sits at $74,780, 10.60 percent below the current level.
That spread is the real state of the market: everything is tight in the short term, while there is plenty of room below before any of the long averages even comes into play. The 20-day average at $83,117 is $409 above the price, the 50-day average $1,029 below it. This week’s trading plays out between those two values.
Bitcoin’s share of the entire crypto market stands at 59.52 percent, with $26.74 billion of turnover in 24 hours. Both readings suggest the money in the market is staying with Bitcoin rather than rotating into smaller coins.
Fed meeting on October 28: the target range stands at 3.75 to 4.00 percent
The Federal Open Market Committee meets on October 27 and 28, with the decision due at 2 p.m. local time in Washington on the Wednesday, 7 p.m. in Germany. The date appears in the Federal Reserve meeting calendar. A fresh round of projections with members’ rate forecasts is not part of it; a press conference by chair Kevin Warsh is.
The target range stands at 3.75 to 4.00 percent. The Fed raised it by a quarter point in September, the first increase in more than three years. On prediction markets the probability of an unchanged range sat between 84 and 88 percent on Tuesday, and between 12 and 13 percent for a further increase. For the December meeting, an increase is priced at around 78 percent.
Phil Camporeale, chief global investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Wealth Management, writes that his team expects no move at the October meeting. His firm looks for around 50 basis points of further increases, spread out into 2027. From inside the central bank, New York Fed president John Williams set out the line that there is no rush.
How a rate-hiking cycle works on the Bitcoin price
Bitcoin has lived through falling or flat rates for most of its existence. A hiking cycle is new for this market, and it works through three channels.
First, the alternative: as the risk-free rate rises, a term deposit pays more, and an asset with no running yield has to make up that head start through its price. Second, financing: anyone invested on credit or with leverage pays more for it, and some of those positions get closed. Third, the dollar: higher rates usually support the US currency, and a strong dollar weighs on the dollar-denominated Bitcoin price.
That third channel hits euro-based holders twice. You pay in euros but convert a dollar price. If the dollar rises against the euro, your loss in euros is smaller than the dollar loss, and the other way round. At $82,708 and 73,652 euros, the implied rate is currently just under $1.123 per euro.
Funding of 0.0034 percent per eight hours equals 3.75 percent a year
The financing rate, known in trading as funding, is the payment that holders of perpetual futures make to each other every eight hours. When it is positive, buyers pay sellers, and the futures market trades above spot.
On the OKX exchange the rate for the Bitcoin perpetual stood at 0.00343 percent per eight hours on Wednesday morning. Annualised, that is around 3.75 percent. The number is notable because it sits almost exactly at the upper edge of the Fed’s target range. A leveraged long currently costs about as much as the risk-free rate in dollars, before the price has moved at all.
That leads to a calculation anyone can run: hold a long position for a year and you need roughly 3.75 percent of price gains just to pay the financing. Over a week that is 0.072 percent, over a month 0.31 percent. For a position meant to run to October 28, it is about 0.07 percent, or $58 per Bitcoin held.
Spot, ETN or perpetual: what makes the difference before October 28
There are three common routes into Bitcoin for European investors, and they behave differently ahead of a central bank date.
Buying real coins on an exchange licensed under the European MiCA regulation costs a one-off order fee and nothing after that. There is no liquidation price, and a ten percent move costs ten percent. Which providers hold a licence and what they charge per order is set out in our comparison of crypto exchanges.
An exchange-traded note, or ETN, tracks the price through a securities account and carries a running management fee. What counts is whether the paper is physically backed with coins or merely replicates the performance. That distinction, and the fee levels of the papers tradable in Europe, are set out in our overview of crypto ETFs and ETNs in Germany.
A leveraged perpetual future costs the financing described in the previous section and comes with a liquidation price. At tenfold leverage and an entry at $82,708, that price sits roughly ten percent away, around $74,400 before fees. Last night’s range was 2.39 percent. Four such nights in the same direction would be enough. What the individual platforms charge in financing is shown in our comparison of perp exchanges.
Our assessment: the inflow came from one provider, not from the market
From the newsroom’s point of view, Monday was weaker than the $526.7 million headline suggests. The evidence is above: IBIT took in $665.2 million, more than the entire net amount, FBTC gave up $83.6 million, and the month remains around $88 million in the red. The Ethereum funds lost $103.3 million the same day. A market buying broadly looks different.
Against that, the origin of the money does not matter for the price effect. A fund taking in $665 million has to buy coins, and that purchase meets the same order book as any other. The price responded with only 0.80 percent in 24 hours, and that says more about the state of the market than the inflow figure itself: there is enough supply on offer to absorb sums like these.
For the week up to the Fed meeting, that suggests fund flows are unlikely to lift the price out of its range. The October 28 decision is the date that can change it, and prediction markets expect no change there. The setback risk therefore lies less in the decision itself than in what Kevin Warsh says about December at the press conference.

articles.summary: ECB Caught In The French Drama - TalkMarkets  Howl.link
articles.full_text:
Back in September, the ECB surprised markets with a more hawkish message, at least between the lines. With headline inflation higher for longer and core inflation expected to increase in 2027, the stage seemed set for at least one more rate hike at the December meeting. Some even speculated about a back-to-back increase in October.
One month later, and after a severe fiscal and political crisis in France, the ECB is unlikely to repeat the hawkish tone at next week’s meeting. At face value, macro developments since the last meeting would still justify another rate hike. Headline inflation increased again in September and most leading indicators point to continued resilience in the eurozone economy. However, the surge in bond yields on the back of the French crisis is already imposing a new restrictive monetary policy stance. In fact, the surge in German bond yields since the September meeting has already had roughly the same impact on growth and inflation as an additional 25bp rate hike. For France, it's closer to a 50bp hike. Or in other words, the bond market has taken over the ECB’s job.
All of this means that the ECB is very likely to stay on hold next week and will delay any next rate hike decision to December. This is when new staff projections will be available and when there will also be more insights into whether higher energy prices will eventually bring knock-on effects on the rest of the economy or not. In fact, there are three main parameters that, in our view, will determine the ECB’s path going forward: i) the length and intensity of the war in the Middle East. The longer oil prices remain elevated, the higher the probability of more rate hikes; ii) the knock-on effects of higher energy prices. So far, there has hardly been any pass-through of higher energy prices in the rest of the economy. If this remains the case, the need for further rate hikes drops. If it doesn’t, the likelihood of new rate hikes goes up. iii) France. Any solution to the current French fiscal woes could bring some relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to continue hiking rates. Without any solution, bond markets have taken over the ECB’s role, making rate hikes less likely (and less needed).
Because it's France
Even if France does not play a role in the ECB’s policy statement next week, it will be an important element at the press conference. Political and fiscal concerns in France, and the resulting widening in French spreads, have raised questions about whether the ECB could intervene through the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which allows it to purchase securities issued by member states whose financing conditions have deteriorated for reasons not justified by country-specific fundamentals. However, before activating it, the Governing Council considers a cumulative set of criteria to determine whether the countries concerned are pursuing sound and sustainable fiscal and macroeconomic policies. In practice, this includes compliance with the EU fiscal framework, which would, at a minimum, require the proposed French budget to be fully adopted.
The ECB has nevertheless left itself some discretion, stating that the intervention criteria “will be dynamically adjusted to the unfolding risks and conditions to be addressed”. This brings back memories of the famous “because it’s France” by former European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker. Generally speaking, the ECB will be in a difficult position: intervening too quickly in support of France may be viewed unfavourably by other member states and interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules. That argues strongly against early intervention. Also, don’t forget that the leadership changes at the ECB over the next months (Schnabel, Lane, Lagarde) could also affect how the ECB views TPI.
Given the challenges of justifying the activation of TPI at present, we expect the ECB to adopt a three-pronged approach to address the French crisis.
- The first line of defence is a more dovish approach to policy rates. As bond markets are currently taking over the ECB’s job of inserting a more restrictive monetary stance on the economy, there is less need for the ECB to hike rates aggressively, or to hike rates at all. In fact, the ECB has already started to prepare for this option, as ECB president Christine Lagarde recently noted that “while growth has been resilient, since our last meeting long-term interest rates have risen notably, which will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise".
- The second line of defence would be a covert return to bond purchases. The ECB could instead pause quantitative tightening temporarily and reinvest maturing bonds in its portfolio 'flexibly', sending a positive signal to bond markets. This had already happened during the Covid period.
- Last but not least, should contagion in eurozone bond markets intensify, we expect the ECB to eventually trigger the TPI. As long as France remains non-compliant with the European fiscal rules, the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France.
All in all, next week’s ECB meeting looks set to be uneventful on action but clearly not on words.

Copper fell to its lowest in more than five weeks on Thursday as further inflows into London Metal Exchange warehouses eased some supply fears, even though expectations of regional supply bottlenecks persisted outside the US.
Benchmark three-month copper on the LME was down 1.8% at $14,089 a metric ton as of 1600 GMT. It hit a session low of $14,031, its weakest since September 15.
Copper stocks in LME warehouses climbed for a fourth day after 29,050 tons of inflows on Wednesday, chiefly in the US storage hub of New Orleans.
Total LME copper stocks now stand at 272,950 tons, the highest since July 24, after earlier flows into New Orleans and Baltimore this week. Around 62% of all LME copper inventories are currently in the US.
Alastair Munro, senior metals strategist at broker Marex, said the recent build in LME copper stocks was the result of the COMEX premium shrinking as contract delivery dates draw closer.
Traders have been shipping copper to the US COMEX exchange for much of this year, attempting to head off potential import tariffs on the metal, pushing COMEX prices higher than LME prices.
However, the front of the curve now shows COMEX trading at a discount to the LME, encouraging flows on to the LME instead. The backwardation on the LME – a market structure where prices for prompt delivery are higher than those further forward – has also incentivised deliveries.
The cash LME copper contract was last trading at a premium of $116 a ton to the three-month forward contract, indicating ongoing near-term tightness.
Elsewhere, sell-off in equity markets on doubts over the AI outlook weighed on the industrial metals complex.
Aluminium fell 1% to $3,010 a ton, zinc lost 2.2% to $3,670 and lead dipped 0.7% to $1,896.50, even after there was an order to withdraw 46,800 tons of the metal from warehouses in Singapore.

articles.full_text:
(Kitco News) - Gold’s disappointing performance in recent months is further proof that it is not a reliable inflation hedge, and while it remains an important diversification tool, one fund manager says investors should be looking at broad-based exposure to commodities as the global economy enters what could be a generational supercycle.
In an interview with Kitco News, Tim Pickering, President and CIO of Auspice Capital Advisors, said that while he personally likes gold and silver, he would not be investing in the precious metals at this time, as persistent inflation and elevated interest rates continue to create significant headwinds.
Pickering explained that gold's biggest weakness as an inflation hedge is that it can become a rate-sensitive investment precisely when consumers are facing rising prices. He noted that this is not the first time gold has been a disappointing inflation hedge. He pointed out that gold struggled between 2020 and 2022, even as U.S. inflation surged to a four-decade high of 9%.
"Gold's not a panacea. It's just a diversifier," he said.
Pickering argued that investors need to distinguish between assets that react to inflation and those that actually drive it. While gold can benefit from monetary uncertainty and changing investor sentiment, energy, industrial metals and agricultural commodities are direct inputs into the global economy.
"Commodities are a source of inflation, not a reaction to it," he said.
The distinction is becoming increasingly important as oil prices continue to trade around $100 a barrel and central banks struggle to contain inflation without damaging economic growth.
Pickering explained that central banks can use higher interest rates to reduce demand-driven inflation, but monetary policy is much less effective at addressing rising production costs caused by higher energy prices, wages and raw materials.
He added that investors should prepare for inflation to remain structurally higher than the unusually low levels seen in the decade following the 2008 financial crisis.
"People need to accept that we're in a world where that type of inflation is normal," he said, referring to annual inflation around 3% to 4%.
Although Pickering remains fundamentally bullish on commodities, including precious metals, he emphasized that investment decisions should ultimately be driven by price trends rather than economic forecasts.
Auspice's broad commodity strategy, which tracks 12 markets, currently holds long positions in nine commodities. Gold, silver and North American natural gas are the three markets without long exposure.
The portfolio instead holds positions in petroleum products, copper, corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton and sugar.
Pickering said the strategy's lack of precious metals exposure reflects their weak price performance rather than a fundamental rejection of either asset.
"I love the fundamentals of silver," he said, adding that he is more optimistic about silver's underlying supply-and-demand outlook than gold's.
"That doesn't mean I'm going to be long. If it's going down all year, my job is to either protect your capital or make you money on the short side."
Pickering noted that Auspice had already been aggressively reducing its silver exposure toward the end of 2025, as the metal's historic rally drove volatility sharply higher. By the time silver peaked in January, the firm had effectively exited its position.
As for what would bring the firm back into gold and silver, Pickering said the answer is relatively straightforward: sustained positive price momentum.
"I'm never going to pick a bottom," he said. "We look for momentum."
He explained that Auspice generally looks for a trend to develop over several months before establishing a position, with exposure adjusted according to volatility and relative portfolio risk.
While gold and silver remain under pressure, Pickering said investors should not confuse weakness in individual markets with the end of the broader commodity bull market.
In fact, he believes the world is only in the early stages of a commodity supercycle that could last more than two decades.
"I think we're six years into a 20-plus-year cycle," he said. "We're in a supercycle, in my opinion."
Pickering identified three structural drivers supporting his long-term outlook: growing consumption from emerging-market middle classes, the global energy transition and rapidly expanding demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers.
He explained that these forces are creating sustained demand for energy, industrial metals and agricultural products at a time when investment in new commodity production has failed to keep pace.
Unlike the commodity boom of the early 2000s, which was largely driven by China's industrialization, Pickering said the current cycle has several powerful demand catalysts operating simultaneously.
"Now you're in a situation where there isn't one catalyst, there's like three core massive catalysts," he said.
Geopolitical instability and supply-chain disruptions are creating additional pressure on already constrained commodity markets, he explained.
Pickering pointed to the conflict surrounding the Strait of Hormuz as an example of how inflationary pressures can spread across the commodity complex.
While the immediate impact has been higher energy prices, he warned that disruptions to fertilizer supplies could eventually affect agricultural production and food prices.
He said farmers may have already secured their fertilizer requirements for this year's growing season, but higher costs could become a much bigger concern in 2027.
These developments help explain why Pickering expects investment capital to continue rotating between different commodity markets rather than concentrating in a single asset.
He noted that money initially flowed into grains at the beginning of the year before shifting toward energy as geopolitical tensions intensified. As energy prices corrected during the summer, investment interest returned to agricultural commodities.
For investors, Pickering said this rotation reinforces the importance of maintaining diversified exposure rather than trying to identify the next gold, silver or oil rally.
The firm's systematic approach uses three primary factors: price trends, volatility-based position sizing, and the structure of commodity futures curves.
Although gold has struggled in the current environment, Pickering said that higher interest rates could create an unexpected source of support for the commodity supercycle, despite their near-term impact on precious metals.
Pickering explained that commodity producers are increasingly competing with technology companies and AI infrastructure developers for investment capital. As borrowing costs rise, mining and energy companies may struggle to finance the production capacity needed to satisfy future demand.
"Structurally higher interest rates is not helping this problem," he said. "It's exacerbating it significantly, in my opinion."
He added that a stronger U.S. dollar does not necessarily prevent commodities from performing well, even though most raw materials are priced in dollars.(Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Meanwhile, Pickering sees the traditional 60/40 portfolio of equities and bonds facing new challenges as persistent inflation weakens the diversification benefits of fixed income.
He said the simultaneous decline in stocks and bonds during 2022 demonstrated why investors should consider alternatives that behave differently from traditional financial assets.
He explained that this is also the philosophy behind Direxion's recently launched U.S. 500 Plus ETF (SPXP), which tracks an index developed by Auspice. The fund combines S&P 500 exposure with a managed-futures strategy spanning commodities, currencies and interest rates.
Pickering explained that the strategy uses capital-efficient futures contracts to maintain equity exposure while adding a separate source of potential diversification through commodities, rather than requiring investors to sell existing stock holdings to make room for alternatives.
Ultimately, Pickering said he does not expect central banks to aggressively raise interest rates to the point of triggering a severe recession simply to return inflation to their traditional targets.
He believes policymakers will increasingly have to accept somewhat higher inflation rather than risk significant economic damage from attempts to control supply-driven price pressures. He noted that although the global economy has gotten used to low inflation since the 2008 Great Financial Crisis, inflation since the 1970s has averaged around 4%.
"You're not afraid of normal inflation," he said. "You're afraid of stagflation."
Although the risk of a recession remains, Pickering said the combination of resilient demand, years of underinvestment and structural growth in commodity consumption should continue to support the broader market.

Key Takeaways
- Nexo reports bitcoin rallied 42.7% in Q3, surging from $58,544 to $83,570 to end a prolonged slump.
- The U.S. Treasury boosted global risk assets by doubling purchases of long-dated bonds in Q3.

Federal Reserve and Inflation: Bitcoin’s Core Drivers
As the global cryptocurrency market enters the final stretch of the year, a new report from digital asset wealth platform Nexo paints a picture of a resilient market finding its footing. Following a third-quarter recovery that broke a prolonged slump, the industry now faces a pivotal fourth quarter where macroeconomic policy, monetary decisions and institutional demand will dictate the next major trend.
The third quarter delivered a much-needed psychological and financial turning point for crypto markets. Breaking three consecutive quarters of negative performance, bitcoin jumped 42.7% after starting the quarter at $58,544 and closing at $83,570.
Altcoins participated heavily in the third-quarter upside, capitalizing on an improved risk appetite. Ethereum outperformed alongside the broader market, racking up an impressive 70.9% gain over the quarter, while Solana appreciated by approximately 60%. Nexo’s data highlights that the primary catalyst for the broad-based recovery was not a crypto-native breakthrough, but a U.S. Treasury announcement that it would double its purchases of long-dated bonds.
This move effectively compressed bond yields and injected vitality back into global risk assets. As selling pressure systematically eased through September, on-chain metrics improved markedly, with the share of bitcoin supply held in profit climbing back to roughly 69%.
While the market backdrop is undeniably healthier than it was midyear, Nexo’s outlook stresses that fourth-quarter performance is far from guaranteed. The market enters the final quarter facing a delicate balancing act between supportive structural indicators and near-term macro hurdles.
At the heart of Nexo’s fourth-quarter outlook is monetary policy. The upcoming Federal Reserve interest rate decision looms large as a definitive catalyst for digital assets. According to the report, the direction of interest rates and incoming inflation prints will heavily dictate whether momentum can sustain itself. A favorable rate decision or a policy hold could pave the way for continued market expansion, whereas unexpected hawkish shifts or persistent inflation could introduce heavy volatility and force consolidation or a pullback.
Mixed ETF Signals and Potential Market Scenarios
Institutional participation remains the cornerstone of modern market cycles, but the fourth quarter has introduced mixed signals. Following the robust capital inflows of the previous quarter, exchange-traded fund (ETF) flows turned net negative in October. This dip highlights underlying market uncertainty and indicates that institutional investors are temporarily pumping the brakes to reassess macroeconomic conditions before committing fresh capital.
Meanwhile, Nexo’s outlook maps out a spectrum of potential paths for the remainder of the year. The primary projection is that bitcoin and major altcoins could resume their upward trajectory, provided monetary policy remains stable or eases. If macroeconomic uncertainties persist, markets may enter a prolonged sideways range as investors wait for clarity on inflation and central bank actions. Conversely, should incoming data surprise to the upside on inflation or force the Fed into a more restrictive stance, risk assets could face short-term downside corrections.
Ultimately, Nexo’s report portrays an asset class that has successfully shaken off its midyear lethargy only to face a high-stakes macroeconomic test. With on-chain health robust and long-term conviction intact, the crypto economy’s immediate trajectory rests on central bank actions and upcoming liquidity signals. For traders and institutional players alike, navigating the final months of the year will require a keen eye on macroeconomic data releases and shifting ETF dynamics.

articles.summary: The situation in the Middle East has deteriorated, and AI‑related trading has cooled, prompting investors to once again seek safe havens; U.S. Treasury yields have hit a near one-month low.  富途牛牛
articles.full_text:
A reassessment of AI‑driven trading prospects is reshaping global asset allocation, with equity markets under pressure prompting investors to flock to safe‑haven assets such as U.S. Treasuries, the Japanese yen, and the Swiss franc. The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury hit 5.38%, its lowest since September 23; the yen strengthened 0.3% against the dollar to 157.68, while the Swiss franc gained 0.2%. Safe‑haven demand emerged even as oil prices rose following the attack on Saudi Arabia, with the next move hinging on whether inflationary pressures or a cooling of AI‑driven trading will take center stage.
Mixed earnings reports from tech stocks, coupled with escalating tensions in the Middle East, have dampened global risk sentiment, bolstering the safe-haven status of U.S. Treasury bonds.
On Thursday, U.S. Treasury yields fell across the board by at least 3 basis points.$U.S. 30-Year Treasury Bonds Yield (US30Y.BD)$It touched 5.36%, the lowest level since September 23. Meanwhile, the Japanese yen and Swiss franc strengthened in tandem, while Australian and New Zealand bond markets also rose, underscoring a clear shift of global capital toward traditional safe-haven assets.
"Recently, market sentiment has turned noticeably fragile, with investors reassessing AI‑related assets," said Eugene Leow, Senior Rates Strategist at DBS Bank. "Questions about profitability and return on investment are quietly gaining traction. With U.S. Treasury yields still near recent highs, investors are leaning toward buying Treasuries as a hedge against risk."
The aforementioned risk-averse buying emerged as oil prices rose following a deadly attack on Saudi Arabia and a shift in the supply outlook, creating a tug-of-war between two opposing forces. BMO Capital Markets warned that, on the eve of the Federal Reserve's October 28 policy meeting, the U.S. Treasury market's narrow trading range may be building momentum for a breakout.
Escalating tensions in the Middle East have heightened supply concerns, pushing international oil prices higher.
In the pre-market session of U.S. stocks,$Brent Last Day Financial Futures (DEC6) (BZmain.US)$The index climbed to 112, hitting a new high since June. Meanwhile,$CBOE Volatility S&P 500 Index (.VIX.US)$A 10% surge.
The immediate trigger for the rise in oil prices came from the Middle East. Following a deadly attack in Saudi Arabia, market concerns about a further escalation of regional tensions and disruptions to crude oil supplies have risen sharply. In response, the U.S. State Department ordered the evacuation of non-essential U.S. diplomatic personnel and their families stationed in Saudi Arabia, citing the ongoing and growing threat posed by Yemen's Houthi rebels.
According to Bloomberg, citing U.S. officials and sources familiar with the matter, the militaries of the United States and Israel have drawn up specific plans for a new round of strikes against Iran following the U.S. midterm elections.
Rajeev De Mello, Global Macro Portfolio Manager at Gama Asset Management, said investors are "uneasy" about oil prices breaching $110. "Oil and energy prices continue to hit new highs, exhibiting clear stagflationary characteristics. As the Northern Hemisphere winter approaches, implied volatility in oil options has risen again, reflecting heightened uncertainty about the trajectory of energy prices."
Earnings reports diverge, and the AI narrative faces pressure.
Before the U.S. stock market opens,$Tesla (TSLA.US)$Down roughly 5%, the company's third-quarter revenue fell short of expectations, and it has lowered its capital expenditure target.
$Semiconductors (LIST2015.US)$Most stocks declined, with IBM down about 5%, Intel down about 5%, Micron Technology down about 3%, and NVIDIA down about 2%.
$Optical Communication (LIST23979.US)$Overall decline, with Marvell Technology down about 5%.
$Meta Platforms (META.US)$Slight gains: the company's Q3 revenue and Q4 guidance both exceeded expectations, the lower bound of AI capital expenditures has been raised, and it plans to issue non‑voting shares.
Tim Waterer, Chief Market Analyst at KCM Trade, said: "The market is currently extremely critical of capital expenditures. Companies' increased spending worries investors, and their reduced spending does too—Tesla is the latest example. In this environment, it's nearly impossible to strike the right balance."
Kaanhari Singh, head of Asia-Pacific equity derivatives sales at Barclays, told Bloomberg Television: "The market is essentially signaling that AI‑driven trading has moved from the stage of hype and narrative speculation to one of rigorous performance validation, with expectations for outperformance now significantly higher—whether in terms of capital‑expenditure guidance or the clarity of monetization pathways."
The core concern among investors today is whether the massive capital expenditures on data centers and computing‑power infrastructure can translate into returns within a reasonable timeframe. Meanwhile, the sharp rally in AI‑related stocks this year has put valuation pressures on hold, and discussions about bubble risks are steadily gaining traction.
Risk-aversion demand has reignited, driving U.S. Treasuries and the Japanese yen higher.
The stock market's decline has served as the immediate catalyst for this round of U.S. Treasury price gains. Growing investor skepticism about the profitability and return on investment of AI‑related assets has fueled equity-market weakness, reigniting demand for Treasuries as a safe haven.
"Market sentiment has recently turned noticeably fragile, as investors begin to reassess AI‑related assets," said Eugene Leow, senior rates strategist at DBS Bank. "Concerns about profitability and return on investment are quietly gaining traction. With U.S. Treasury yields still hovering near recent highs, investors may be seeking to hedge some risks by purchasing government bonds."
The yen's performance further underscores the broadening of risk-aversion sentiment.$JPY/USD (JPYUSD.FX)$The yen appreciated 0.3% to 157.68, while the Swiss franc also gained 0.2%. David Forrester, a strategist at Crédit Agricole, noted, "S&P 500 futures lower have provided upward momentum for the yen. Importantly, this rally has been broad-based, even extending to the yen's performance against the U.S. dollar, underscoring that the yen's safe-haven status remains intact amid headwinds from the AI boom."
With the Federal Reserve meeting approaching, U.S. Treasuries may face a directional breakout.
Technical indicators suggest that the consolidation phase in the U.S. Treasury market may soon be coming to an end. In a report released on Wednesday, BMO Capital Markets noted that the Bollinger Bandwidth has narrowed sharply from 80 basis points on September 28 to just 24 basis points; such a compression in market volatility often signals that a more pronounced directional move is imminent.
"To some extent, the current price action's sideways pattern suggests a breakout is imminent," BMO strategists wrote in a report.
$U.S. 2-Year Treasury Notes Yield (US2Y.BD)$As the most sensitive to monetary policy expectations, the yield has closed between 4.70% and 4.82% on every trading day since October, with a narrow range of just 12 basis points. However, intraday volatility has at times widened to as much as 27 basis points, and the average daily move since October has risen to 10 basis points—the highest monthly average since March this year.
BMO expects the Federal Reserve to hold interest rates steady at its October meeting and then raise them by 25 basis points in December. However, market pricing for a rate hike within the year may already be overly confident—implied odds of a December hike stand at roughly 90%—and with new economic data coming in, this outlook remains subject to significant revision.

SHANGHAI: China’s yuan extended gains to reach its highest level in more than four years against the dollar on Thursday, underpinned by broad greenback weakness overnight, as investors re-assessed the US interest rate outlook amid renewed oil-driven inflation concerns.
Attention is now turning to a series of major central bank meetings next week, with the Federal Reserve, the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank all expected to leave rates unchanged while maintaining a hawkish stance.
Prior to the market opening, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) set the midpoint rate at 6.7195 per dollar. The spot yuan is allowed to trade 2% either side of the fixed midpoint each day.
Thursday’s midpoint was 439 pips weaker than a Reuters estimate of 6.6756 - its largest weak side deviation since September 23.
The central bank has been gradually strengthening its daily yuan official guidance this year, but at levels weaker than market expectations, suggesting it is seeking to manage the pace of appreciation, traders and analysts said.
“The fixing stance had not shifted with PBOC leaning against the speed of the USD/CNY decline as spot trades below fix,” Maybank analysts said.
“The spot-fix gap has not widened substantially and that suggests that PBOC is allowing the current direction of travel to continue.”
In the spot market, the onshore yuan touched a high of 6.6740 per dollar at one point, the strongest level since June 2022, before changing hands at 6.6749 as of 0238 GMT.
Its offshore counterpart last fetched 6.6744 yuan per dollar, up about 0.01% in Asian trade.
Trading was thin, with onshore spot prices hovering in an extremely tight range of about 20 pips and trading volume shrinking to about $10.6 billion.
Currency traders said strong exports and sustained foreign-exchange settlement have underpinned the yuan this year.
With the yield differential between China and the United States near its widest level on record, investors are closely watching the path of US interest rates for direction on the Chinese currency.
Fed funds traders see only a small chance of a Federal Reserve hike next week, with the next interest rate increase expected in December.
“If export proceeds and foreign exchange settlements continue, the yuan can remain stable or even appreciate while the US dollar index maintains its resilience,” analysts at China Merchants Bank said in a note.

articles.title: One interest rate, three inflation realities. Why Europe’s price shock is so uneven - Euronews.com
articles.summary: One interest rate, three inflation realities. Why Europe’s price shock is so uneven  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Finland, Germany and Lithuania share the euro and the ECB’s 2.50% deposit rate, but with September inflation at 2.7%, 3.3% and 6.1% respectively, they show how one policy meets different price realities.
Three countries share one currency and one central bank rate, yet their inflation rates differ by more than twofold.
In September, annual inflation was 2.7% in Finland, 3.3% in Germany and 6.1% in Lithuania, according to Eurostat’s harmonised index (HICP), published in October. The euro-area average was 3.8%. All three face the same European Central Bank (ECB) deposit rate of 2.50%.
An energy shock felt unevenly
The common thread is energy. Eurostat data show energy prices across the euro area rose 18.9% in September, adding 1.71 percentage points to inflation, almost half the headline figure. Excluding energy, euro-area inflation was 2.3%.
How that shock plays out depends on a country’s energy mix, tax choices and the strength of its domestic economy.
Lithuania: energy, taxes and wages
Lithuania sits at the top of the range, and food is not the reason. Eurostat figures show food, alcohol and tobacco inflation at 0.5%, while energy prices jumped 33.0% and services inflation reached 6.9%.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) attributes the surge to elevated energy prices amid continued import dependence, strong domestic demand and higher excise duties. Policy added to the pressure. From January, Lithuania raised the VAT on residential heating, hot water and firewood from 9% to 21%. The government’s draft budget estimated that the heating change alone would add 0.5 percentage points to inflation.
Pressure has spread beyond fuel and heating. Eurostat data put Lithuania’s core inflation, excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, at 3.9%. The Bank of Lithuania expects average wages to rise 9.4% in 2026, and the European Commission links services inflation to strong pay growth and an 11.1% rise in the minimum wage.
Higher wages may leave many workers better off on average. But pensioners, benefit recipients and low-income households with large energy bills are more exposed. There is also a second-round risk. Labour-intensive service businesses can pass higher wages into prices, keeping inflation elevated after the energy shock fades.
Finland: cushioned and sluggish
Eurostat figures show Finland faced a similar energy shock, with energy inflation at 13.1%, yet headline inflation stayed at 2.7%. The European Commission says Finland’s relatively low reliance on fossil fuels softened the blow. Statistics Finland found that cheaper electricity and owner-occupied housing costs restrained its national consumer price index, even as petrol, diesel and heating oil pushed it up.
Domestic price pressure is weak. According to Eurostat, core inflation was 1.4% and services inflation 1.7%. The Bank of Finland forecasts 10.4% unemployment in 2026, while the Commission expects GDP growth of 0.8%. Statistics Finland reports nominal earnings rose 3.5% year on year in the third quarter, or 1.2% in real terms.
That combination helps explain why another rate rise may seem overly restrictive from Helsinki.
Germany: a spike concentrated in fuel
Germany falls in the middle. Eurostat data show energy inflation at 13.4% and core inflation at 2.5%. Germany’s statistics office, Destatis, found motor fuels up 37.1% and heating oil up 74.9% in the national index. Excluding those two items, inflation was 1.8%.
Wage pressure is moderate. Negotiated wages rose 2.9% year on year in August, and the Bundesbank projects the same average for 2026. Eurostat puts services inflation at 2.8%.
Policy also muddies the picture. Existing federal measures lowered electricity, gas and district-heating prices, and a new fuel-tax cut took effect on 1 October, so it is not included in September’s figures. National interventions can shift measured inflation monthly without changing the underlying European shock.
What a single rate means
The ECB raised its deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.50% in September, arguing that the Middle East conflict was keeping inflation above target and that the full effects of the energy shock had yet to emerge.
Subtracting national headline inflation from the ECB rate gives a rough real-rate proxy: minus 0.2% in Finland, minus 0.8% in Germany and minus 3.6% in Lithuania. This simple calculation based on ECB and Eurostat figures is not a true measure, since households and firms act on expected inflation and face different borrowing costs.
The policy tensions differ by country. Finland’s weak growth and high unemployment argue against tightening. In Germany, the rate is easier to defend given core inflation of 2.5%, but September’s acceleration was driven almost entirely by fuel and heating oil. In Lithuania, the rate looks loose against 6.1% inflation, though higher rates cannot reverse a VAT increase or lower imported fuel prices. They work by weakening demand and curbing second-round effects.
Transmission also varies. ECB research finds that policy works faster and more strongly where variable-rate debt and household leverage are more common, and Lithuania is among the countries relying on variable-rate mortgages with short reset periods.
Yet a recent study covering 2000 to 2025 suggests output and inflation responses to monetary policy are less uneven than often assumed, as some structural differences offset each other.
Sources: Eurostat, ECB, IMF, European Commission, Bank of Lithuania, Bank of Finland, Statistics Finland, Destatis, Bundesbank.

articles.title: On the Chain: Bitcoin holds near US$83,000 as volatility sinks ahead of Fed decision - Proactive financial news
articles.summary: On the Chain: Bitcoin holds near US$83,000 as volatility sinks ahead of Fed decision  Proactive financial news
articles.full_text:
Bitcoin is holding around US$83,000 as cryptocurrency markets enter an unusually quiet period ahead of next week’s US Federal Reserve decision, despite renewed institutional buying through BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency was trading around US$82,860 at the latest check, after moving between US$82,567 and US$84,786 during the current session.
Bitcoin has spent much of the past week between US$80,000 and US$84,000, with traders showing limited willingness to take large positions ahead of several major macroeconomic events.
The consolidation follows a volatile start to October in which Bitcoin briefly traded above US$87,000 before higher inflation, rising Treasury yields and cryptocurrency fund withdrawals pushed it back towards US$80,000.
Volatility drops towards 2026 low
Bitcoin’s 28-day realised volatility has fallen to around 1.2%, close to its lowest level of 2026.
Trading volumes have also softened as investors wait for clearer direction from interest rates and financial markets.
The Federal Reserve is due to make its next rate decision on October 28, with markets currently placing a high probability on rates remaining unchanged.
US inflation remains above target, limiting the Fed’s ability to ease policy even as parts of the economy and labour market show signs of slowing.
Bitcoin has become increasingly sensitive to expectations around interest rates because high Treasury yields offer investors a comparatively attractive return without the volatility associated with cryptocurrencies.
BlackRock buying returns
Institutional demand nevertheless remains an important source of support.
US spot Bitcoin ETFs attracted around US$527 million in net inflows in one recent session, their strongest daily result in almost a month.
BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for more than the entire net gain, attracting roughly US$665 million while funds operated by Fidelity and Grayscale experienced withdrawals.
The scale of the BlackRock buying suggests institutional interest remains resilient even as Bitcoin struggles to break above its recent trading range.
Bitcoin ETF flows had weakened considerably earlier in October following two consecutive weeks of withdrawals.
Ethereum rebounds above US$2,500
Ethereum was trading around US$2,507 at the latest check, up almost 3% over 24 hours after moving back above the psychologically important US$2,500 level.
Ether has been supported by increasing staking activity, although its US-listed ETFs have experienced persistent withdrawals during October.
XRP was trading around US$1.37, gaining more than 4% over 24 hours, making it one of the stronger major cryptocurrencies during the latest session.
Solana was near US$108.35, up roughly 2.4% over 24 hours but still well below levels above US$120 reached earlier this month.
The broader cryptocurrency market has consequently improved even as Bitcoin remains trapped within its recent range.
Breakout pressure building
The unusually low volatility suggests Bitcoin may be approaching a larger move.
Support remains concentrated around US$80,000-US$81,000, an area that has repeatedly attracted buyers during October.
On the upside, Bitcoin needs to establish itself above US$84,000 before another challenge of the US$85,000-US$87,000 region becomes likely.
A sustained move through US$87,000 would put US$90,000 back in focus, while a decisive break below US$80,000 would represent a significant deterioration in the current market structure.
For now, Bitcoin is effectively waiting for a catalyst.
With volatility close to its lowest level of the year, BlackRock buying aggressively and the Federal Reserve decision approaching, the current calm may prove difficult to sustain.

articles.title: Elon Musk reportedly invests $1bn in David Ellison’s Skydance
articles.summary: Musk’s investment into the new media empire comes after Paramount’s $111bn merger with Warner Bros DiscoveryElon Musk has reportedly invested approximately $1bn in Skydance, the new media empire led by David Ellison.The deal comes alongside fresh equity infusions from existing investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow. Semafor first reported the news. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk has reportedly invested approximately $1bn in Skydance, the new media empire led by David Ellison.
The deal comes alongside fresh equity infusions from existing investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow. Semafor first reported the news.
The investment follows Paramount’s recent $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery, a huge acquisition that brought the media companies together under the Skydance name. At the head of the new media empire is David Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison.
The Guardian has contacted Musk and Skydance for comment.
The cash infusion solidifies an alliance between two of Trump’s richest monetary backers. In September, Semafor reported that Paramount executives had considered Musk as an equity investor, citing his close ties to Larry Ellison, who invested $1bn in Musk’s acquisition of X in 2022 and also $45m in support of Trump’s re-election bid in 2024. Musk spent more than $290m on Trump’s re-election bid and has spent more than $350m backing Republicans in the current US midterm elections.
After the merger, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, who previously led Mattel, informed employees that the integration would involve layoffs, stating: “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce.”
The company’s leadership – which now oversees Paramount and Warner Bros’s movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN – has set a target of more than $6bn in cost savings over the next three years, a goal that Los Angeles county officials estimate could lead to the loss of 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles alone.
Prior to the merger, a coalition of 12 states, including California and New York, sued Paramount, arguing that the deal would “extinguish” competition and result in “higher prices, lower quality and less content for film and television”.
In September, a settlement agreement required Skydance to release at least 30 films and more than 180 television shows annually, while ensuring that CBS and CNN maintain editorial independence.

articles.title: Meta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill
articles.summary: Chief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth taxMeta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires.The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California, where Meta’s headquarters are located. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires.
The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California, where Meta’s headquarters are located.
Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or wherever Meta maintains its base, for eight years.
Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40, a one-off 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state.
Zuckerberg, worth $239bn (£180bn) according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.
In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders. This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of these new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company.
Recent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaires have been spending heavily to fight the measure, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel and the former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has described Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs.
“Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay,” Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week.
“In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened.”
Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn. But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’s lawsuit over child protection and social media addiction failings.
The company’s shares slid by more than 6% when trading opened on Wall Street on Thursday, helping to drag the tech-focused Nasdaq index down 2.5% amid a wider selloff of AI-linked stocks.
In a separate case, on Wednesday a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn following a trial that found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data.
Meta also revealed that it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago.
Reuters contributed to this report.
